articles.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
articles.summary:
A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November

AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Read more

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

Read more

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

Read more

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

articles.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
articles.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

articles.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
articles.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

articles.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
articles.summary: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

articles.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
articles.summary: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

articles.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
articles.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

articles.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
articles.summary: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

articles.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
articles.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

articles.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
articles.summary: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

articles.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
articles.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

articles.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
articles.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

articles.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
articles.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

articles.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
articles.summary: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

articles.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
articles.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

articles.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

articles.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
articles.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

articles.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
articles.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

articles.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
articles.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

articles.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
articles.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

articles.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
articles.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
articles.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

articles.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
articles.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

articles.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

articles.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
articles.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

articles.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
articles.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

articles.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

articles.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

articles.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

articles.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

articles.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
articles.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

articles.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
articles.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

articles.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
articles.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

articles.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
articles.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

articles.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

articles.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
articles.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

articles.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

articles.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.

articles.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.summary: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed exec with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair, is a Chinese spy.

articles.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
articles.summary: Elon Musk's social network X has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see on the platform.

articles.title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
articles.summary: From reading more books to breaking mindless scrolling habits, Apple's foldable has changed my daily routines in ways I didn't anticipate.

articles.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.

articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.summary: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.summary: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.

articles.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
articles.summary: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck last month, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared to 65.5 days for trucks overall.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.

articles.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
articles.summary: The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.

articles.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
articles.summary: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
articles.summary: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.

articles.title: X’s latest update for creators focuses on vertical video
articles.summary: As short-form video ramps up in popularity, X's new creation tools are part of its effort to compete with YouTube and Instagram.

articles.title: WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
articles.summary: Users can schedule messages from 10 minutes later to after 14 days.

articles.title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
articles.summary: ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck.  ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. […]

articles.title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.summary: The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

articles.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach
articles.summary: Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.

articles.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
articles.summary: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.

articles.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
articles.summary: The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang's affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances.

articles.title: Yale’s Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a ‘detriment’ to US industrial might — not a champion
articles.summary: Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld warns that what the market cheered Monday, Jensen Huang's White House–backed return as Nvidia's CEO and board member, could prove a giant mistake, exposing the directors to "historic" personal liability from a growing pile of lawsuits and raising the question of whether the country is celebrating a company that has helped put advanced chips in its adversaries' hands.

articles.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
articles.summary: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.

articles.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
articles.summary: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.

articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
articles.summary: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.

articles.summary: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.

articles.title: The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
articles.summary:
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has hit a new low price just a few months after release. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Black Friday is entering the evening, which means one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch is coming to a close. After all, the holiday savings can help offset the unfortunate price hikes from earlier this year, when Apple raised the cost of some of its most popular gear. Some discounts still apply to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, too, which are available at their lowest prices to date.

In addition to a variety of discounts across retailers, Apple is offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases between November 27th and November 30th. How much you get back is determined by how much you spend, with up to $100 available for some iPhone and Apple Watch purchases, and up to $300 for the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That said, in some cases you may be able to save more by buying from other retailers.

Earbud and headphone deals

AirPods Pro 3

The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$249 $149 at Amazon

$249 $149 at Walmart

$249 $149.99 at Best Buy

Beats Powerbeats Pro 2

Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$249 $179.95 at Amazon

$249 $179.95 at Walmart

$249.99 $179.99 at Best Buy

You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review.

The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Target also has them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.

Beats Studio Pro

The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$349.99 $139.95 at Amazon (select colors)

$349.99 $99 at Walmart (select colors)

$349.99 $139.95 at Best Buy (select colors)

Beats 360 headphones

The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$349.99 $249 at Amazon

$349.99 $249.99 at Best Buy

If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are on sale starting at $79.99 ($120 off) at Amazon and Target — a new low price. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.

The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review.

MacBook deals

MacBook Neo

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$799 $699.99 at Amazon (512GB, Touch ID)

$699 $649 at Best Buy (256GB)

$699 $599 at Amazon (256GB)

Apple MacBook Air (M5)

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$1299 $999 at Amazon (13-inch, 512GB)

$1299 $999 at Best Buy (13-inch)

$1499 $1199 at Amazon (15-inch, 512GB)

The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,099 ($300 off) — a new low price — at Amazon. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.

The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,749 ($250 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price. The Pro builds on its predecessor with a faster chip and support for Wi-Fi 7. In our testing, it handled multitasking, photo editing, and occasional video editing with ease while still delivering exceptional battery life. It lacks the newer MacBook Pro’s gorgeous OLED display, but its Mini LED screen still looks great, especially given its smooth 120Hz refresh rate. It also offers excellent speakers and a good selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SD card slot. Read our review.

Apple Watch deals

Apple Watch Series 12

The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$399 $299 at Amazon (GPS, 42mm)

$399 $329 at Best Buy (GPS, 42mm)

$449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm)

The Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration starting at $179 ($50 off) at Amazon and Walmart, matching its best price to date, while Best Buy is currently $20 higher. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. Read our review.

Apple AirTag (second-gen)

Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batteries.

It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $599 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro. Read our review.

Apple’s latest Magic Mouse is matching its all-time low of $59.99 ($20 off) at Amazon. Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank

The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

Where to Buy:

We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date.

The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game.

The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify.

articles.title: Buying a laptop right now is rough, but these Black Friday deals help
articles.summary:
Affordable laptops are even more affordable right now. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Laptop prices have been a hot-button topic all year long thanks to RAMageddon. We’ve seen existing models get more expensive and new models arrive at higher prices than last-gen — sometimes with lower specs, too. 2026 in general has been a bad time to buy a computer. But thankfully, Black Friday can offer a tiny bit of respite.

If the computer you currently use is working well for you, good. Happy for you. But if you’re in the market for something more powerful, bigger, smaller, thinner, etc. — and you prefer new over used — you can currently save some decent dough on MacBooks, Windows notebooks, and gaming laptops.

The big, multi-hundred-dollar savings are typically reserved for higher-end models with bigger specs, like Windows models running Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark platform — which are getting their first major discounts. articles.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
articles.summary:
Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

articles.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
articles.summary:
Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it.

articles.title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
articles.summary:
In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.

Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.

articles.title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
articles.summary:
One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.

Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

articles.title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
articles.summary:
About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

articles.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
articles.summary:
Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

Losing its voice

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

articles.title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.summary:
According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.

The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.

“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.

articles.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
articles.summary:
The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.

That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.

As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.

It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.

Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.

articles.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
articles.summary:
Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

A handful of teeth with a lot to say

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

articles.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
articles.summary:
Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.

articles.title: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
articles.summary:
My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don't meet your daily driving needs. It's tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you're holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren't hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what's currently playing in your browser.
Credit:
Nick Indge

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in "the drawer."

Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device.
Credit:
Nick Indge

Installation is a doddle

Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn't have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you'd like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

articles.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic

Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.

Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.

articles.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
articles.summary:
On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

articles.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
articles.summary:
“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.

This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.”

Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.

articles.title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
articles.summary:
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The Legarda-Leviste solar empire: From government contracts to private billions
articles.summary:
Behind Leandro Leviste’s entrepreneurial success lies a corporate strategy that converted government-awarded development opportunities into marketable equity, generated billions in financial transactions, and left substantial contractual obligations unresolved.

Leandro Leviste was undeniably innovative, though his commercial ingenuity extended well beyond the technology of generating solar power. His corporate strategy demonstrated how exclusive renewable-energy development rights granted by the government could acquire enormous financial value even before some of the projects underpinning them delivered electricity. (READ: Leviste solar companies passed around DOE deals as franchisee incurred losses)

Did the Filipino public receive economic benefits commensurate with the private wealth those state-granted opportunities helped create?

In the first installment, Vantage Point examined the Anti-Money Laundering Council’s (AMLC) allegations concerning Senator Loren Legarda, former Energy secretary Alfonso Cusi, and Leviste in the acquisition and retention of solar development rights. 

We now trace what happened after those rights were secured: how corporate assets were consolidated, how shares were monetized, and how billions subsequently moved through Leviste’s personal accounts. 

The corporate strategy centered on Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc. (SPPPHI), Leviste’s principal investment vehicle. In February 2022, a reported asset-for-share swap involving interests in 20 solar project companies and associated assets (See list of these companies below this paragraph) was structured around roughly 24.37 billion shares of SP New Energy Corp. (SPNEC), valued at P2.50 apiece. That translated into a transaction valuation of approximately P60.93 billion, subject to the terms and completion of the share exchange. (See list of these companies:

Solar Philippines Calatagan Corporation

Solar Philippines Tarlac Corporation

Solar Philippines Tanauan Corporation

Terra Solar Philippines, Inc.

SP Holdings, Inc.

Solar Philippines Batangas Baseload Corporation

Solar Philippines Tarlac Baseload Corporation

Solar Philippines Central Luzon Corporation

Solar Philippines South Luzon Corporation

Solar Philippines Southern Tagalog Corporation

Solar Philippines Eastern Corporation

Solar Philippines Western Corporation

Solar Philippines Visayas Corporation

Solar Philippines Central Visayas Corporation

Solar Philippines Southern Mindanao Corporation

Solar Philippines Batangas Corporation

Solar Philippines Retail Electricity, Inc.

Laguna Solar Rooftop Corporation

Solar Philippines Rooftop Corporation

Solar Philippines Commercial Rooftop Projects, Inc.

To be clear, this was not P60.93 billion in cash earnings. Still, it illustrates how development rights, corporate interests, and related assets could be packaged into marketable equity capable of attracting institutional capital. A privately held portfolio had found a direct pipeline for monetization through the stock market. 

The entry of Meralco PowerGen Corp. (MGen) gave that pipeline substantial financial muscle. In 2023, its renewable-energy arm, MGreen, injected P15.9 billion into newly issued SPNEC shares—capital that flowed directly into the listed company. Subsequent deals involving existing shares and exchangeable financing arrangements, however, provided funding opportunities for Leviste’s corporate vehicles as selling shareholders or borrowers. (READ: Leandro Leviste sells another P3 billion in SPNEC shares as solar controversies mount)

By June 2025, Leviste had announced completed and agreed share transactions totaling P20.49 billion, comprising P18.26 billion involving the MGen group and P2.23 billion from earlier sales to public investors. His widely publicized P34-billion funding target included prospective deals and financing arrangements and should not be mistaken for fully realized personal cash-outs.

SPNEC investment and share transactions

Source: SPNEC June 25, 2025 PSE clarification. MGen group deals and public sales total P20.49 billion.

Monetization continued even after Leviste entered Congress. On August 20, 2026, SPPPHI offloaded another 2.4 billion SPNEC shares at P1.25 apiece, raising P3 billion in gross proceeds and paring its common-share stake from 16.30% to 11.51%. Eight days later, SPNEC’s board approved the acquisition by its wholly owned subsidiary, Terra Nueva Inc., of land from Provincia Investments Corp. and JJPNM Agro Industrial Corp.—both subsidiaries of SPPPHI.

As Vantage Point previously reported, the land acquisition disclosure omitted the purchase price, acreage, and valuation methodology. While there is no established link between the share sale and the proposed land purchases, minority shareholders deserve full transparency on the terms under which Leviste’s private firms continue transacting with the listed company as his equity stake shrinks. 

The AMLC’s financial investigation adds another layer to the picture. According to reported Court of Appeals records, Leviste’s accounts logged roughly P28.07 billion in inflows and P29.82 billion in outflows, representing P57.89 billion in cumulative financial activity. Investigators also flagged 1,044 checks totaling roughly P14.99 billion issued to Leviste by his solar companies, raising concerns about the possible commingling of corporate and personal funds.

Reported financial activity in Leviste’s accounts

Source: Reported AMLC findings in Court of Appeals proceedings. The P14.99 billion in checks is not added to this total

Here, the accounting principle is fundamental. Corporations have legal personalities distinct from their shareholders. Funds transferred to an owner must rest on a clear accounting and legal basis—whether as dividends, loan repayments, advances, or other legitimate transactions. Owning a corporation does not automatically make its cash the owner’s personal property.

Leviste maintains that all transactions were lawful and undertaken in the ordinary course of business. Assessing that claim requires a line-by-line reconciliation of corporate ledgers, bank statements, tax filings, and underlying contracts. Gross transaction volume alone does not establish unlawful enrichment. (READ: Leviste denies he made money from selling franchise to Pangilinan’s Meralco group)

(Editor’s note: Tony La Viña, the spokesman of Senator Loren Legarda and Representative Leandro Leviste, has spoken up on the solar controversy in this clip: Watch:

Meanwhile, major contractual commitments went unmet. The AMLC identified roughly P10.44 billion tied to 26 terminated renewable-energy contracts. Separately, the Department of Energy (DOE) pegged its broader aggregate demands against Solar Philippines, its subsidiaries, and affiliates at P24 billion. Because the two figures cover different scopes and may overlap, they should not be combined—nor do they represent final judicial awards. (READ: DOE: Only 0.3% collected from P24 billion in penalties vs Leviste’s Solar Philippines)

Just as importantly, these reported obligations should not automatically be pinned on today’s SPNEC. Under MGen’s stewardship, MTerra Solar Phase 1 began commercial operations in August 2026, initially declaring 600 MWac under its Meralco power-supply agreement. That represents tangible project delivery, and the capital and execution risks shouldered by the new controlling shareholder deserve due recognition.

Must Read

Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal

Similarly, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s inquiry into alleged franchise flipping demands legal precision. Solar Para sa Bayan’s congressional franchise is legally separate from the DOE service contracts held by other Solar Philippines entities, and MGen has denied acquiring shares in the franchise holder. Whether any transaction circumvented statutory restrictions remains a question for investigators to address. 

The Court of Appeals’ freeze orders remain provisional safeguards, not convictions. What the government must now establish is straightforward: which corporate entities owe money, where the proceeds of monetization went, and whether the individuals behind unfulfilled obligations can be held legally accountable. (READ: Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste face plunder, graft complaints over solar projects)

In renewable energy, the true measure of entrepreneurial success is electricity delivered to the grid—not merely shares sold or paper valuations achieved. Government development rights are instruments of national energy policy, not unconditional entitlements to private fortune. Filipinos are owed a transparent accounting of both sides of the ledger: what private enterprise gained from public privileges and what the nation received in return. – Rappler.com

Source note: This analysis draws from reported AMLC findings contained in Court of Appeals proceedings, SPNEC’s Philippine Stock Exchange disclosures and corporate filings, Department of Energy pronouncements, statements from the parties concerned, and previous Vantage Point investigations into Solar Philippines and SPNEC.

articles.title: Saving reefs: Coral Triangle expedition makes its way to the Philippines
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – The Tara schooner makes its stop in the Philippines as part of its 18-month expedition in the Coral Triangle, attempting to understand why and how corals in the region are resisting climate change.

The storied schooner, built for polar drift in 1989 with its round aluminum hull, will be making stops in Araceli, Palawan, and Puerto Galera, Mindoro. It arrived in the Philippines on November 20 and docked at the Manila Yacht Club.

“It appears that coral reefs in the region seem to have a resistance and resilience potential that’s higher than everywhere else in the world, but we can’t explain really why,” Martin Alessandrini, advocacy officer of Tara Ocean Foundation, told reporters aboard the schooner on Thursday, November 26.

“It’s really a ray of hope for coral conservation, but we need to better understand it in order to better protect these corals.”

The Coral Triangle covers the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Solomon Islands, and contains majority of the known coral species in the world. It is known as the Amazon of the Ocean.

After leaving France at the end of 2025, the schooner crossed the Atlantic to reach the Pacific via the Panama Canal. Its first public stopover was in Tokyo, Japan, in April 2026. Prior to the Philippines, researchers in the schooner had stopped and collected samples from the waters of Papua New Guinea and Palau.

The team in the schooner mainly works on sampling. After collection, they send the samples to different laboratories for analysis. It takes two to three years after the expedition “to produce all the data and the very first results,” said Alessandrini.

SAMPLING. Divers from the Tara schooner take coral samples in Palau.

Climate change has triggered coral bleaching events, threatening marine habitats around the world. Four global coral bleaching events have been recorded since 1998, according to a recent report from the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network, with each event “associated with a 6.5–9.9% relative loss of global hard coral cover.”

Tara Ocean Foundation, based in Paris, France, supports the expedition and has partnered with the UP Marine Science Institute and non-profit organization Blue Alliance. The expedition vessel was designed by French naval architects Olivier Petit, Luc Bouvet, and engineer Michel Franco.

Inside the schooner

The vessel is manned by six sailors and eight scientists.

Below the cockpit is a common area where the staff holds meetings. In the kitchen are at least two packs of dry yeast and a KitchenAid stand mixer.

“Yes, we make bread everyday,” Alessandrini said as he toured reporters in the vessel. “It’s a French boat, so we need bread and we need good food.”

Further along are the sleeping quarters and bathrooms. There is a bookcase at the end of the hallway, lined with works of great authors.

The storage area beyond the sleeping quarters houses the watermaker (“to produce drinking water from seawater”), generators, and food stocks in huge containers.

All diving equipment is stored at the back of the boat, where coral samples are also kept and conserved.

“We take sediments around the corals,” Alessandrini explained. “We take fragments of corals also. And we take cores of corals, which help us understand the previous climate in the region.”

Filipino on board

Three Filipino researchers are slated to join the expedition at intervals during its Philippine leg.

Vince Nikko Ordinario, 27, is the first to join the team heading for Palawan. Ordinario, a research assistant at the UP Marine Science Institute, said he will be in the vessel for 40 days.

SIGNAGE. The entrance to the cockpit is decorated with art and signages. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

“I joined to help this expedition, get data, analyze,” Ordinario told Rappler in the schooner. “Then I can take it home to the laboratory. We can use the data in the laboratory.”

Two other Filipino researchers are joining in the latter half of the Philippine leg. After their stops in Palawan and Mindoro, the team would have been done with five out of the total nine sampling sites they intend to visit in the expedition.

Following the public stopover in Manila, the schooner is scheduled to stop by Kuala Terengganu, Malaysia, in July 2027 and then in Singapore in August 2027. – Rappler.com
