articles.title: 2027: Odii vows to end poverty, industrialise Ebonyi
articles.summary:
From Jude Chinedu, Enugu

The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ebonyi State, Chief Ifeanyi Odii, has vowed to tackle poverty, industrialise the state and create jobs.

He accused the incumbent administration of failing to translate increased federal allocations into improved living conditions.

Odii, who spoke at the flag-off of the PDP governorship campaign in Abakaliki, said the state’s growing revenue had not translated into the expected development and improved welfare for residents.

He argued that governance should be measured by its impact on the people rather than the amount of money received or spent by government.

The PDP candidate identified poverty, poor rural roads, inadequate healthcare facilities, limited economic opportunities and lack of access to clean water as major challenges facing the state.

He claimed that national assessments indicated that nearly eight out of every 10 Ebonyi residents were living in multidimensional poverty.

Odii also faulted inadequate investment in agriculture, arguing that a state whose economy depended largely on farming could not justify allocating less than two per cent of its 2025 budget to the sector.

He questioned the utilisation of funds earmarked for education, particularly those meant for teachers’ training and children’s educational needs.

He further expressed concern over Ebonyi’s weak industrial base despite its abundant mineral resources. He noted that farmers continued to face difficulties while the state remained heavily dependent on federal allocations.

He promised that his administration, if elected, would prioritise industrialisation, economic diversification, job creation and accountable governance.

“Government must be measured by how much it has improved the lives of the people,” he said.

Recalling his participation in the 2023 governorship election, Odii alleged that he was denied victory despite winning the poll.

He, however, expressed confidence that the 2027 election would provide another opportunity for residents to elect their preferred leaders.

The rally attracted thousands of supporters from the state’s 13 local government areas.

PDP National Chairman, Abdulrahman Muhammed, who attended alongside members of the National Working Committee, presented the party’s flags to Odii, his running mate, Patrick Mgbebu, and other candidates.

Muhammed described the turnout as evidence of the party’s grassroots strength, and urged residents to support its candidates in the National Assembly, governorship and State House of Assembly elections.

Also speaking, PDP National Secretary, Senator Samuel Anyanwu, expressed confidence that Odii would win across the state’s 171 electoral wards and 13 local government areas.

The post 2027: Odii vows to end poverty, industrialise Ebonyi appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Our govt’ll unite Nigeria, fight insecurity-Obi
articles.summary:
From Okey Sampson, Umuahia

The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr Peter Obi, said on Friday evening in Aba, Abia State, that the government he would run with Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso would unite Nigeria and fight insecurity to a standstill.

He however said for the government that will usher in a new Nigeria to emerge, leaders like the incumbent President, Bola Tinubu, must be shown the exit door.

Mr. Obi who stated these in Aba, Abia State during a Town Hall meeting stressed that Tinubu had gone against his campaign promises and had subsequently plunged the entire country into an abyss of poverty.

He assured the crowd that the government he was seeking to form would not only unite Nigeria, but would transform all sectors of the country beyond their current state.

Obi said the presidency requires energy and must not be turned into a retirement home for tired persons.

“Tinubu has failed to fulfil all his promises, including the restoration of the power sector. We will generate, transmit and distribute at least 10,000MW. Any money we borrow must be for investment.

“The presidency requires energy; it is not a retirement home. We are tired of Tinubu’s government. Tinubu must go for a better Nigeria to emerge.

“Let me assure you that the government Kwankwaso and I are seeking to form will unite Nigeria. Yesterday (Thursday), I was in Minna, and I told them that Nigeria used to be united. No wonder Nnamdi Azikiwe and Chukwuemeka Ojukwu were born in Zungeru, Nigeria State.

“The Nigeria we want is one where a child of nobody can become somebody without knowing anybody.”

He criticized the Tinubu administration for borrowing more money than all previous governments combined, while it has nothing to show for it.

“Kwankwaso and I want to form a government that will not give you excuses. We already know the excuses, and we will tackle the challenges. Our government will demonstrate compassion, commitment and the zeal to get the job done.

“We will fight corruption. Public money will be used for the public good. In the past, Nigeria borrowed money to build projects such as the Kainji Dam. Today, we borrow for nothing.

“We now have more poor people than China and India put together. Our youths are heavily unemployed. We want to form a federal government that will invest in education and healthcare.”

He assured the people of Abia State that Aba, the commercial capital, would become an export hub and would be linked with Port Harcourt to create a new economic hub within the first few years of their administration.

On insecurity, Obi said, “We cannot be in government while schoolchildren are being kidnapped and others taken into the bush. We will be in that bush with them.”

He thanked residents for coming out in large numbers to meet him.

The post Our govt’ll unite Nigeria, fight insecurity-Obi appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Political violence may truncate Nigeria’s democracy – Pogu, MBF leader
articles.summary:
•Why Middle Belt leaders endorsed Tinubu

•Nigeria needs restructuring for all to have a sense of belonging

 

President of Middle Belt Forum (MBF) Dr. Bitrus Pogu, has warned that the escalating political violence over the 2027 elections may truncate Nigeria’s fledgling democracy.

According to him, the country is witnessing a vicious cycle, noting that the same technique the political class used against former President Goodluck Jonathan is now being used against President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, who was part of the opposition, and a beneficiary.

In an interview with VINCENT KALU, the MBF leader stressed that the AI generated photos in the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) register is enough to trigger serious problems before and after the election. He therefore called on the electoral umpire to come clean by presenting the staff involved for prosecution to allay the fears of the opposition parties.

How can you describe the 2027 elections campaigns?

The campaigns have not been normal because of all the violence associated with it, and all sorts of things. We thought that each of the presidential candidates, particularly, should have free space to express themselves, whether people like it or not. All the associated violence doesn’t augur well for the election proper.

Our politics is becoming more militant, and that is unfortunate. The other positions, the Senate, the House of Representatives, nobody really pays attention to what they are doing. Everybody is paying attention to the presidential campaigns or flag off. So far, it hasn’t been impressive; it isn’t the appearances or the speeches, but what attracts more attention is the so-called violence that is associated with the campaigns and it’s unfortunate, and we don’t want to go on that trajectory.

What do these violent attacks portend for the elections and the country’s democracy?

It’s going to be a sad situation if we are not careful; if it is not controlled right now, it would mean that the election proper would be full of violence and the election would be a do or die affair.

If we are not careful, they may set the whole country ablaze, and that would certainly truncate our democracy.

We pray that we don’t degenerate to that position because the way things are building up and the way the judgment of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), which up to now seems to leave the party in a horrible situation, are serious issues. All these would continue to build up into real frustration and maybe, and unfortunately, it might result into violence even before the election, because as we are talking, the David Mark faction under which the former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is contesting still doesn’t have a place on the INEC ballot given that it is the Gombe faction that has the party.

So, if this is not resolved, that alone is enough to ignite something which we will not be able to contain. It’s unfortunate, but the law has taken its real course. Nobody can challenge the court, given that they based their judgment on the party’s constitution that says if the chairman is removed, it’s the deputy who takes over. So that alone has to be managed, whether the government and the judiciary will decide to use political settlement rather than judicial settlement. I know that.

Whether or not INEC would soon open its portal to admit the contestants of a harmonised ADC, we don’t know. But whichever way it goes, that alone is enough to ignite violence, let alone the election proper.

And given the kind of atmosphere and what we have been watching, not edited, the raw news coming out, the Bamaso slogan and whatever, whether they are genuine or sponsored, they are not a good indicator of a good, peaceful election. And we also pray that all the issues around INEC will be resolved early enough, otherwise, all those would be brought to bear when violence erupts, and we pray we don’t degenerate to that situation.

Since this political dispensation from 1999, Nigeria has never experienced this level of violence, threats, intimidation. What brought about it?

The political class has been a bit desperate in their approach as we moved on. The same All Progressives Congress (APC), which today is in power, wrestled power from a peaceful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) government of Goodluck Jonathan in 2014. If you remember, since then, we have gone downhill in this direction.

At that time, they were falsely accusing the sitting government of Jonathan, as being responsible for the insurgency that was bedevilling the country. Now, the insurgency, instead of reducing, increased and went beyond the North East, where it was to all other parts of the country, especially the North Central Zone and the North West.

The same technique, which was used against Jonathan is now being used against President Tinubu. At that time, he was a beneficiary because he was part of the opposition.

Today, it is being used against him and the same characters, majority of them were part of this government. The presidential candidate of ADC now was also part of the system or the group that pulled Jonathan down. So, you can see that it is a vicious cycle. It is the political class that’s responsible; people are so desperate.

Of course, there are some other developments, which were not there before. Because of insurgency, many Hausa people have started to feel and believe that the Fulani are killing them.  For example, Hausa Zalla and Hausa Tsansa. Hausa Zalla means all, while Hausa Tsansa means the committed Hausa. These are movements that have appeared in the North. The Hausa are saying that Fulani have dominated us; Fulani are killing us, and that religion has nothing to do with it, we want to own our political space. It has never been there before now, and now it is there.

So, all these ones are now contributing to the overall problem of the country.

The economic policies have brought immense hardship on Nigerians and coupled with the increase in insurgency, abductions, payment of ransom, etc. All these have brought a lot of frustration and people without reason feel it is the government in place that lacks the capacity or is unwilling to resolve the issues.

These have all compounded the situation resulting in the unnecessary violence we are seeing out there. We just pray that people will see reason.

If in 2014, when they were accusing Goodluck Jonathan, they came to discover that it wasn’t Jonathan that was responsible, but elements who feel Nigeria has to belong to them and have used insurgency for political purposes, I think people will start reasoning well.

So, the propaganda machinery of the government and all those who are campaigning out there has to come out in full swing to educate people to know exactly where these things are coming from; where the insurgency is coming from and secondly, with regards to the economic policies of government, it is up to Mr. President and his team to know how to control it because that’s a factor in this violence.

What do you have to say about the campaign messages?

It is not a policy-based campaign. Yes, different groups have some different issues they are depending on. For example, Mr. President is claiming that his reform programme is going to pay off.

Yes, Nigerians have not seen the payoff, but that is what they are dwelling on, and then trying to debunk, especially what the other two principal contestants – Obi and Atiku  – are saying.

Atiku is dwelling mainly on bringing back subsidies, something Nigerians would want to hear, given the economic situation on ground.

Peter Obi is dwelling on his track records that he and he alone has the capacity to right the wrongs in the economy, in the insecurity, etc.

So, the issue here is beyond these statements by the individual. It is all about attacking what this other person is doing rather than coming out with a full-blown policy statement and saying I am coming in because I want to do XYZ. There are some other players who are doing very well, but they don’t have a strong home base like the man of the SDP, Adebayo. Anytime I listen to him, I feel yes, this is a material. So, we have such out there, but the issue is that much of the campaign is not policy-based; they are just mainly trying to attack the opponent; trying to debunk what the opponent has said etc.

The campaign organisations need to do better so that we can begin to see policy-based things. And if the president has written, rather than wasting time about what Atiku or Obi is saying, let him churn it out, and ask us to go and verify what he has done in this, and that sector. That may work better with regards to the issues that should dominate the campaign, rather than fighting each other; trying to undermine each other, etc.

The opposition parties are shouting over the AI-generated photographs in the INEC register. What will it bring about in the 2027 elections?

Those things have to be addressed immediately because it means that things have already gone one direction before even the election has started. We cannot use artificial intelligence just because technology is available. We should rather use AI to help us verify the authenticity of the electorate, and to ensure that people who are underage, people who have registered multiple times, etc are not allowed to participate.

Technology is good, but using it negatively portends a real challenge to the election of 2027, and unless it is addressed convincingly, INEC has already become a suspect in this matter.

Unless it is convincingly addressed so that the fears of the opposition can be allayed, I think that alone is enough to trigger serious problems before and after the election.

If it is not addressed convincingly even after the election the result will not be acceptable and it is unfortunate. The earlier INEC does something about it the better. All the directors of INEC should be able to address the issues at the state level and at the national level so that electronic voting, electronic transfer etc would be so transparent that nobody should query or be given the room to query the outcomes, otherwise it portends serious challenges to the credibility of our elections.

As INEC had admitted that some people within the commission imported these AI-generated photographs, don’t you see this as an alibi for any of the opposition parties if they lose the election to reject the results; they may cite that INEC was hand in gloves with the ruling party to rig the election?

Yeah, that is true. I repeat, INEC should come out clean. They have their advisers, they have their lawyers, and they should sit down, and as a team, convince Nigerians that there was no cause for alarm. The earlier that is done, the better for the country. Otherwise, we may find ourselves in a very tight and difficult situation before and after the election, especially the presidential election.

As advice, the chairman of INEC should do everything within its powers to do what is needed. If there are people who deliberately did that for whichever or whatever reason, they should be brought to book to convince Nigerians that, yes, there is no collusion or support from the INEC leadership to do that or to attempt to do something funny in the future.

That is necessary for the election to be acceptable and to be credible, and for the opposition to be happy with the kind of result that might come out. They should be more transparent in what they do so that there will be no room for suspicion during the election, after taking necessary actions to allay the fears of the opposition at this stage.

The Middle Belt leaders, led by retired Lt Gen T. Y. Danjuma (Retd), penultimate week, paid a visit to President Tinubu and endorsed him for 2027. Is it a new dawn for the region, or was there a political agreement entered into?

It was a pragmatic decision. Why did I say it was a pragmatic decision?  A group in a political dispensation would look at its situation, what its interests are and then take a decision based on such interests. We believe that the presidency should still remain in the south.

Secondly, we believe that in doing so, it will be good for the country, because if, for example, knowing that there is an unwritten agreement that there should be rotation between the north and the south, and if someone from the north, especially now the contestant of ADC, is able to defeat Mr. President, we will all be in trouble because we may end up with something close to June 12.

We considered all this and the interest of the organisation and our people, and we felt that Tinubu should finish his four years so that Nigeria will have peace and not to, because of some sentiments, we then allow the untoward to happen, get ourselves in trouble.

It was based on pragmatic consideration that the decision was taken. I was on the team that went with the Lieutenant General, who is our leader.

If you remember, in 2023, we all came out; we told our people we were going to vote for Mr. Peter Obi, and these leaders supported him along with all of us. But this time, we considered that it is in our collective interest that this man should conclude and complete his term so that we have a peaceful Nigeria going forward.

Four years isn’t going to terminate anybody, and we felt that if peradventure, otherwise happens, that is to say, Atiku comes in, we may not end up well. So, it is out of the love for Nigeria and pragmatic approach to the political issues that that decision was taken. And, of course, our leader led us to make that pronouncement.

We still respect and love Peter Obi, who we supported in 2023, but our pragmatic consideration led us to this position.

Following the visit and endorsement, some political analysts have been wondering, what has changed in the Middle Belt Region, as the killings that escalated since 2023 have not been tackled?

No, no, no. We know that those killings are still there; we know that those challenges are still there. But just as I told you, pragmatism looks at the situation as it is; weigh the options, and decide which of the options is better at this point in time.

In pragmatism, a table can become even a chair, if need be, because you need something to sit on. So, it was such a consideration. Yes, we know these challenges are there, but we believe that it is in our collective interest to allow this man to continue. You will come and find out that our brothers are going to vote for the ADC candidate massively.

So, we felt pragmatically that it is in our collective interest that we support Mr. President to complete the remaining four years in office in spite of the fact that these challenges are still there, we believe they are surmountable.

There were deals of course he had to enter in. Remember, when he came into office in 2023, nearly all of the leadership of the security organisations were controlled by the Fulani -the NSA, Fulani; Minister of Defence, Fulani; Minister of State Defence, Fulani. There was a change only after the minister of Defence was changed and substituted with somebody from the Middle Belt, and some changes came in when the service chiefs were tinkered with. I believe that in 2027 this is not going to be the case. So, we weighed all these things and we felt yes, we love our Obi, but we have to be pragmatic and deliberate in our actions so that we, who have been keeping Nigeria together, will continue to play that role.

When the Northern elders say that they gave Tinubu the highest number of votes, about seven million votes that made him win the election, are they talking about the entire 19 states?

That’s what they claim. It is still unfortunate that some of our governors, even in the Middle Belt Region, continue to subscribe to the defunct Northern Region. That’s why the sultan would invite the 19 northern governors and give them directives to pay N1 billion monthly for 12 months for something called the Northern Security Trust Fund.

That is something we don’t want in this country, because if those regional blocs continue to dictate the direction of Nigeria, we are in trouble. We have moved forward.

Right from the time of Gowon, when he created 12 states and then gradually now, we have 36 states plus the FCT, we have moved forward.

We shouldn’t be allowing regional blocs to dictate what we do because it pertains to fractionalisation of the country along those fault lines, which took us to the civil war, which we don’t want to repeat.

Yes, when they claimed there was a contribution of seven million votes, it included everybody and if you subtract the Middle Belt contribution to fold however small, it amounts to a big chunk. Even in Kaduna, Southern Kaduna is part of us; even in Kebbi, the Zuru part of Kebbi was part of the Middle Belt and it is still part of the Middle Belt because they were part of Niger Province of old. It was the Irikife Panel that moved them to the North West to provide manpower. In the North East, we have areas that are still part of us who they lay claim to.

So, the issue of political propaganda; talking figures did not start today. The rigging started right from the constituency delineation since when states like Kano were having lots of local governments and even when Jigawa State was taken out, Kano still has 44 local governments, and lots of constituencies. The Middle Belt and down south have been rigged out even before the election. Look at the whole of Nasarawa North, right from Nasarawa, Egon, Akwanga, coming down to Wumbi, right into Wamba, up to the border with Plateau State; the whole area that is Northern Senatorial District has only one House of Representatives, one senator, and we have such within us, and yet they would select a place which favours them even one local government and make it a federal constituency just to manipulate the system in their favour.

Nigeria needs rejigging; Nigeria needs restructuring, whether we like it or not, the truth has to prevail. It’s going to be painful to those who have been taking advantage of this lopsided structure. But whether we like it or not, it just has to happen for Nigerians to have a sense of belonging for those who have been cheated, emasculated, manipulated over the years.

Nigeria is better off when equity, fairness, and justice are the norm rather than this manipulative system which operates.

The post Political violence may truncate Nigeria’s democracy – Pogu, MBF leader appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Ibadan: Fear, anxiety over robberies in commercial taxis
articles.summary:
• Commuters worry as taxicabs become security nightmare

A woman, whose name is withheld for security reasons, thought she was taking an ordinary taxi ride from Eleyele to Onireke, Ibadan.

She boarded a commercial Nissan Micra near Unity Hospital at about 9.50am on October 1, 2026, expecting to arrive at her destination without incident. But something went wrong along the way.

By the time she found herself in Oje, she realised that some of her belongings were missing, including her iPhone 11 Pro, valued at N240,000; N2,500 in cash and clothes worth about N10,000. The total value of the missing items was put at N252,500.

 

 

More than a month later, on November 4, she was heading to work when she sighted a Micra taxi she believed she had boarded on that October morning.

She also recognised two occupants, whom she said were in the vehicle during the earlier journey. This time, she raised the alarm.

Her action attracted the attention of people around the area, who helped apprehend the two men. They were subsequently handed over to the police.

The suspects were identified as Gbenga Olubade, 42, and Oluwaseun Adeoye, 50. The Oyo State Police Command confirmed their arrest, saying detectives took the passenger, the driver and another occupant to the station for investigation.

 

Taxicabs in Ibadan

 

According to the command, it received a distress call at about 9.30am on November 4 over a confrontation between a commercial taxi driver and a passenger at TCTC Junction, Idi Ope, along Eleyele Road, Ibadan. Police operatives responded to the report and took the persons involved to the station.

The police said statements had been obtained and that the suspects made confessional statements. It added that investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances of the incident and determine whether the suspects were connected to other criminal activities.

Meanwhile, the case has again drawn attention to growing concerns surrounding the use of commercial Micra taxis in Ibadan and other parts of Oyo State.

For many residents, the small, affordable cars are an important part of daily life. They provide convenient transport along busy routes and connect neighbourhoods that may not be easily served by larger commercial buses.

From Eleyele, Sango and Mokola to Bodija, Ojoo, Akobo, Challenge, Ring Road and Iwo Road, Micras are a familiar sight.

But accounts from some commuters suggested that the same convenience could become a source of danger when criminals exploit the public’s dependence on the vehicles.

Passengers have also recounted incidents involving suspected armed robbery, theft, abduction and attempts to extort money.

In some cases, victims said they were lured into vehicles by people posing as passengers or transport workers. Others alleged that they were threatened with guns and forced to surrender their belongings.

But thousands of drivers depend on the business to earn a living, and many commuters use the service every day without incident. But the allegations raise questions about passenger safety, the monitoring of commercial vehicles and the effectiveness of measures meant to keep criminal elements out of the transport system.

A gun pointed at passengers

One of the accounts involved two commuters, who journeyed from Ojoo to Mokola in Ibadan. They arrived at a filling station beside the Mokola flyover on a commercial motorcycle and intended to board another motorcycle to Iyaganku.

Some Micra taxis were parked in front of the filling station, calling out destinations to attract passengers. Some were announcing Oke-Padre, others Molete, Apata, and Challenge.

As the two men walked past one of the vehicles, a man standing beside it called their attention, saying someone inside the taxi wanted to speak to them. They looked towards the car. According to one of the victims, an occupant pointed a gun at them while the man outside ordered them to enter or risk being shot. They had little choice but to obey.

The vehicle made a U-turn under the bridge at Mokola Roundabouts and headed towards Sango. The occupants dispossessed the two men of a laptop, cash and other valuables before ordering them out of the vehicle and driving away.

The victims said they shouted for help after being dropped, but nobody pursued the vehicle. They also claimed that they did not see any police personnel around the scene at the time.

Earlier accounts of abduction

In May 2022, the case of Oluwafemi Edem, an operations analyst based in Oyo State, was reported in the media. He said he was kidnapped after boarding a Micra taxi in Ibadan.

Edem was reportedly on his way to visit his younger sister at Joke Plaza, Bodija, when he boarded the vehicle. He sat at the back with another passenger, while another person later joined them.

According to the account, Edem lost consciousness around the General Gas Bridge in Akobo. He later regained consciousness in Ogun State, almost naked and wearing only shorts and a singlet. His hands were tied with a rope. He said he managed to untie himself and escape.

Another case was reported in May 2021, which involved a woman identified as Jolayemi Ajuwon, a pseudonym used to protect her identity.

She alleged that she narrowly escaped a kidnapping attempt at Eleyele Bus Stop, along Sango Road, on May 15, 2021, at about 10pm.

According to her account, she boarded a Micra with four occupants, including the driver. The other passengers were women, a circumstance that initially made her feel safe. But she became suspicious because of the way the occupants were seated and decided to get out of the vehicle.

She crossed the road, only for another Micra to arrive. One of its occupants pointed a gun at her. She jumped into a gutter and crawled towards a nearby filling station, where she was able to contact her sister and find safety.

In October 2024, a case was also reported on ‘one-chance’ encounter involving a resident of Olodo, in Lagelu Local Government Area, identified as Akeem Adekunle.

The report described his experience after boarding a Micra taxi heading towards Ojoo. While the details of the different accounts vary, they point to a recurring concern.

How Micra taxis entered Ibadan’s transport system

The administration of former Governor Adebayo Alao-Akala introduced an intra-city taxi scheme in October 2009.

Investigation showed that the then government purchased 200 cars from Asia for the scheme. The initiative was designed to provide taxi services, empower unemployed graduates and improve urban transportation.

The taxis became popularly known as Micra taxis and subsequently gained considerable acceptance among commuters.

Over the years, Micra taxis became a familiar feature of Ibadan’s urban transportation network. Their relatively small size and ability to navigate narrow roads made them attractive to operators and commuters.

They gradually became prominent on several intra-city routes, alongside commercial buses and other forms of public transportation.

By 2016, reports started coming up that though Micra taxis held sway in Ibadan for years, it also raised concerns about their roadworthiness and compliance with traffic regulations.

Eight suspects arrested – Police

The Oyo State Police Command said it is intensifying efforts to address security concerns involving commercial Micra taxis.

The Police Public Relations Officer (PPRO) for the state, Olayinka Ayanlade, said the command was working with relevant ministries and stakeholders to improve the safety of passengers and sensitise both drivers and commuters.

According to him, the police had also deployed intelligence operatives to identified black spots and strategic locations across Ibadan to identify and dismantle criminal networks  using commercial transport as a cover.

“These proactive measures have yielded significant results in recent months, leading to the arrest of no fewer than eight suspects linked to different criminal syndicates involved in these nefarious activities,” Ayanlade said.

He said the police would continue to engage the Park Management System (PMS) to improve intelligence gathering and identify people, using commercial Micra operations to commit crimes.

He appealed to residents to provide timely and credible information that could help the police identify criminal elements and prevent further incidents.

The police spokesman also advised passengers to be cautious about conversations with strangers in commercial vehicles, particularly discussions involving financial transactions, unexpected business opportunities or monetary incentives. Such conversations, he warned, could be tactics used by criminals to identify and exploit unsuspecting victims.

Ayanlade also advised anyone, who suspects that he or she is in a vehicle with armed robbers or fraudsters.

“Passengers who find themselves in a vehicle with suspected armed robbers or fraudsters are strongly advised not to engage in physical confrontation or take unnecessary risks in an attempt to resist their attackers.

“Where possible, they should remain calm, avoid provoking the suspects, prioritise their personal safety and seek the earliest safe opportunity to escape before promptly reporting the incident to the nearest police station or through the Command’s established emergency channels.”

He stressed that human life should take precedence over the recovery of stolen property.

PMS raises alarm, points to vehicle identification

The Park Management System has also acknowledged receiving reports of criminal activities, involving commercial Micra taxis.

Alhaji Olaide Afunleyin, Chairman of PMS, Sango Park, Terminal Two, Iwo Road, Ibadan, said the reports were not new to the transport management body.

“We have also received information about some people using Micra taxis to do evil. It did not happen just today. It has been on for a long time,” he said.

Afunleyin said one of the measures introduced by the Oyo State Government was the sale of identification stickers to commercial public vehicles, including Micra taxis operating in the state.

He said the current stickers carry the Oyo State Government logo and the inscription, ‘Oyo State Park Management System 2026’. According to him, they also contain a QR code, the image of a taxi painted in the state’s brown and yellow colours, as well as a registration code linked to a particular park in a local government area.

He explained that a code, such as YNF RC. 189 indicated a vehicle registered under Lagelu Local Government, while BDJ referred to Bodija in Ibadan North Local Government Area. EGB, he said, represents Egbeda Local Government Area.

The PMS chairman for the unit urged passengers to pay attention to vehicle identification before boarding.

“People should be very careful when boarding taxis in Ibadan and other parts of the state. Any taxi that is not painted in the colour of Oyo State, they should not bother to board it.

“Then, they should also check the registration code of the vehicle before boarding. They can even snap it and send it to a loved one before boarding,” he said.

Afunleyin also disclosed that commercial drivers could themselves become victims of criminals, who disguise themselves as passengers.

He said some suspected criminals chartered a Micra taxi and, after reaching a lonely location, would try to dispossess the driver of the vehicle.

But it was observed that the existence of identification stickers and registration codes does not, on its own, answer every question about enforcement.

Challenge of policing commercial transport

Oyo State had previously taken steps to capture information about commercial transport operators.

In November 2021, Governor Seyi Makinde launched the Oyo State Security and Data Planning initiative, which was designed to collect information about commercial vehicle operators, including their biometric details, vehicle particulars and routes of operation.

The exercise covered different categories of commercial vehicles, including Micra taxis, minibuses and heavy-duty vehicles.

At the launch, the government said the information would be kept in a centralised database to support security planning and monitoring of commercial transport operations.

The initiative was intended to make it easier for security agencies to identify operators and trace vehicles involved in criminal activities. The governor also warned at the time that commercial operators, who failed to register would be regarded as operating illegally.

The Park Management System has since been used to organise commercial transport activities across the state’s 33 local government areas.

Also, the state government has taken other steps to regulate road transport. On June 5, 2026, Makinde signed Executive Order No. 002 of 2026 on the Regulation and Enforcement of Vehicle Registration and Traffic Management.

The order strengthened the state’s vehicle registration and traffic management framework. The governor also announced restrictions on commercial motorcycle operations between 10.30pm and 5.30am. The restriction applies to commercial motorcycles and should not be confused with a curfew on Micra taxis.

Park managers must clean the system

For Professor Oludayo Tade, the problem requires a combination of stronger park-level monitoring, public vigilance and intelligence-led policing.

Tade, a Professor of Criminology,  Victimology and Security Studies, University of Ibadan, said park managers had an important responsibility to identify and remove criminal elements from the transport system.

“The park managers will have to step up their task force to clean the system of bad eggs,” he said.

He advised commuters to board vehicles at designated parks, rather than informal loading points, where it may be more difficult to establish the identity of drivers and other occupants.

Tade also enjoined passengers to be particularly careful when boarding vehicles in isolated locations and at vulnerable periods, especially early in the morning and late at night.

But he said the responsibility should not rest on commuters alone.

Security agencies, he argued, should make better use of information provided by previous victims to identify patterns, trace suspects and uncover criminal networks.

He acknowledged that victims might report similar experiences at different times and locations, but unless the information is properly documented and compared, opportunities to identify repeat offenders might be lost.

Tade stated that a passenger, who reports a suspicious vehicle, its registration details, route or occupants could provide information that becomes useful in another investigation.

He added that the same applies to drivers, who report passengers who hire vehicles under suspicious circumstances or attempt to divert them to isolated locations.

Commuters caught between convenience and caution

For many residents, avoiding Micra taxis altogether is not a realistic option. The vehicles remain an affordable and convenient means of getting around Ibadan, particularly for people travelling short distances or connecting between major transport routes.

A passenger, who boards a commercial vehicle should not have to fear that the journey could end in an armed robbery or abduction.

According to him, the challenge is to ensure that criminal elements do not take advantage of the trust commuters place in public transport operators.

He added that passengers could also take precautions. They should, as much as possible, board at recognised parks or established loading points, check the vehicle’s registration details and share them with family members or trusted contacts. They should be wary of drivers or occupants who make unusual demands, change agreed routes without a convincing explanation or introduce suspicious financial offers.

The police have urged members of the public to report suspicious activities through established emergency channels.

The Oyo State Government has also publicised the toll-free number 615 for reporting security and related concerns.

The allegations, for legitimate Micra drivers, posed another problem. It is about the risk that public confidence in the entire business could be damaged by the actions of a few people.

The Chairman, Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Oyo State Council, Akeem Babatunde Abas, appealed to transport unions and park managers to have a direct interest in identifying suspicious operators and ensuring that their members comply with registration and identification requirements.

“I can say that the November 4 arrest of two suspects has shown the importance of public vigilance. A victim, who recognised a vehicle and its occupants and raised an alarm, which led to the apprehension of two men and a police investigation, is good. But it is an isolated case.

“I must say that isolated arrests will not be enough if the conditions that allow criminals to operate remain unchanged.

“The security agencies must establish the facts in reported cases, investigate possible links between suspects and prosecute those against whom sufficient evidence is found.

“Also, the PMS must ensure that its registration and monitoring arrangements are effective. The government must also make clear how passengers can verify commercial vehicles and where complaints should be directed.

“Above all, the public needs to see that reports are taken seriously and that action follows.

“Micra taxis are part of Ibadan’s everyday transport system. They should remain a means of getting people safely to work, school, markets and home, not a source of fear for the very commuters they are meant to serve,” Abas stated.

articles.title: Pete Edochie: His life, fame and legacy
articles.summary:
Some actors become famous for the characters they play while others have a presence so commanding that they gradually become characters in the collective imagination of a nation. Pete Edochie belonged to the rare latter category.

For decades, the veteran actor occupied a special place in Nigerian entertainment, embodying kings, chiefs, fathers, community leaders and men of authority with an uncommon gravitas. His deep, resonant voice, deliberate delivery, stern facial expressions, imposing carriage and mastery of traditional proverbs made him one of the most recognisable figures in Nollywood and African cinema.

Whether delivering a warning, settling a dispute, addressing his household, or defending the honour of a community, Edochie had a way of making audiences sit up.

His words often sounded less like dialogue and more like pronouncements from an leader whose authority cannot be questioned, and one whose pronouncement are not open to negotiation.

Fondly called Ebubedike, Ononenyi and the Great Iroko, the actor was much more than a screen patriarch. He was a broadcaster, storyteller, cultural ambassador and one of the faces that helped give Nigerian filmmaking a distinct identity.

His death on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at the age of 79, after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer, has left the entertainment industry mourning a man whose career stretched across generations. With his passing, Nollywood has lost one of its most enduring pillars; a man whose influence was felt not only through the films he made but through the standard of presence, discipline and artistry he brought to the profession.

The boy from the North with Igbo roots

Born Peter Uwadiegwu Ogugua Edochie on March 7, 1947, in Zaria, Kaduna State, to an Igbo family from Akamnato, Ifite Nteje, Anambra State, Edochie’s formative years were shaped by the cultural diversity of northern Nigeria.

His father worked with the Nigerian Railway Corporation, a job that exposed the family to different communities and places. Growing up in the North, Pete attended St. Patrick’s and St. James Primary Schools in Zaria before proceeding to St. John’s College, Kaduna.

Although he spent much of his childhood in the North, his Igbo identity remained an important part of his life. The cultural exposure he gained growing up among people of different backgrounds would later contribute to the richness and depth with which he interpreted characters, particularly those rooted in traditional African societies.

Edochie was not born into Nollywood, neither did acting initially seem like the obvious path to fame. His early interests included literature, broadcasting and performance. As a teenager, he developed an appreciation for drama and staged scenes from William Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice while still in school. It was a glimpse of a talent that would eventually find a much bigger stage.

Broadcasting: The career before the fame

Long before audiences began addressing him as Chief, Ebubedike or the Great Iroko, Edochie was a young man making his way in the world of radio.

He joined the Eastern Nigeria Broadcasting Corporation in February 1967 as a junior programmes assistant, beginning a broadcasting career that would span more than three decades. His entry into the profession came after he discovered that the invitation for his employment interview had arrived after the scheduled date. Rather than surrender to the disappointment, he went to the station to plead for another opportunity.

That persistence opened the door to a career that would take him through several levels of responsibility and eventually into senior management.

At the station, Edochie developed the discipline, communication skills and understanding of storytelling that later become invaluable to his acting career. He rose through the ranks, working in broadcasting during a period when radio remained one of the most influential channels of information, entertainment and public engagement in Nigeria.

He later became Director of Programmes at the Anambra Broadcasting Service and also served as Deputy Managing Director, occasionally acting as Managing Director.

His broadcasting years were not merely a prelude to acting; they were an important part of the foundation of his craft. They taught him the power of voice, timing, articulation, and audience engagement—qualities that later become defining elements of his performances. During the Nigerian Civil War, he also worked with the Voice of Biafra. This experience formed part of his history as a broadcaster during one of the country’s most turbulent periods.

For Edochie, the microphone came before the camera, and the professional discipline he learned in broadcasting followed him throughout his life.

Okonkwo: The role that changed everything

Every legendary actor has that one role that permanently alters the course of their career. For Pete Edochie, it was Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s literary masterpiece, Things Fall Apart.

In 1987, his portrayal of the proud, uncompromising and tragic Igbo warrior catapulted him into national prominence and introduced his talent to a much wider audience. The production, based on Achebe’s celebrated novel, required an actor capable of carrying the emotional weight, cultural complexity and contradictions of one of African literature’s most iconic characters.

Edochie delivered.

He embodied Okonkwo’s ambition, temper, pride, fear of weakness and desperate attachment to the traditions of his society with remarkable conviction. His performance captured the character’s strength while exposing the vulnerabilities beneath it, the insecurities, the anger, the fear of failure and the tragedy of a man who was unable to adapt to a changing world.

The role became so closely associated with him that, for many viewers, Pete Edochie and Okonkwo seemed inseparable.

Interestingly, accounts of how he secured the role reveal that his casting was not simply a matter of fame or connections. His physical carriage, manner of walking and ability to interpret the character impressed the production team during auditions. Edochie, surprisingly, said he had not read Achebe’s novel before encountering the script, making his eventual performance all the more remarkable.

The impact of Things Fall Apart went beyond Nigeria. His performance drew international attention, with the BBC sending a team to interview him following the success of the production. At a time when Nigerian television productions were still fighting for wider international recognition, Edochie’s portrayal of Okonkwo became one of the performances that demonstrated the power and possibilities of African storytelling. It was a defining moment. The broadcaster had become a star.

From television icon to Nollywood royalty

Following the successful adaptation of Things Fall Apart, Edochie gradually established himself as one of the most sought-after actors in Nigeria’s emerging film industry.

As Nollywood expanded from its early productions into a powerful continental entertainment force, he became one of the actors audiences could readily identify with quality, gravitas and commanding screen presence.

His filmography includes notable titles such as Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire’s Club, Egg of Life, Oduduwa, Last Ofalla, Sins of the Father, Across the Niger, The Staff of Odo, Sacred Tradition, Idemili, and Lionheart, among others.

In Igodo, he brought his familiar authority to a story deeply rooted in traditional belief, communal sacrifice and the spiritual complexities of African society. In other films, he played men whose decisions carried consequences for their families, kingdoms or communities.

His casting became almost a genre of its own. Producers knew what Edochie brought to a film: a face audiences trusted to carry authority, a voice capable of commanding a room and a performer who could give weight to dialogue that might otherwise have felt ordinary.

But his artistry was not limited to playing men with titles. Behind the imposing persona was an actor capable of conveying emotional tension, pride, pain, betrayal and the quiet struggles of family life. His characters were often powerful, but also flawed, stubborn, vulnerable, and sometimes tragically human. His ability to command attention without resorting to excessive theatrics helped distinguish him from many of his contemporaries.

The man who made proverbs a cinematic trademark

Perhaps one of Pete Edochie’s most enduring contributions to Nigerian pop culture was his mastery of proverbs and traditional expressions.

In countless films, he delivered words of wisdom, warnings and philosophical reflections that audiences repeated long after watching the movies. His lines often carried the rhythm and weight of traditional storytelling, drawing on the wisdom of elders, community values, and the lessons of everyday life. For younger viewers who may never have sat through a village meeting or listened to an elder settle a family dispute, his films offered an introduction to the language, customs and moral framework of traditional African society.

He became particularly associated with Igbo proverbs and expressions, delivering them with the confidence and precision of a man who understood not only their meaning but also, their cultural significance. His famous screen mannerisms – the slow turn of the head, the deliberate pause, the raised eyebrow, the stern look before a pronouncement – became part of his signature.

Over time, his acting style inspired imitation, parody, skits and countless social media memes. Younger comedians and content creators borrowed his mannerisms to create humour. At the same time, his voice and expressions became instantly recognisable even to people who could not recall the titles of his films. That ability to cross generations, moving from serious cinema to internet culture, was a testament to his extraordinary reach.

A patriarch on screen, a family man at home

Away from the cameras, Edochie was a husband and father whose family life was a significant part of his identity. He married Josephine Edochie on March 19, 1969, at St. Finbarr’s Catholic Church in Umuahia, Abia State. Their marriage lasted more than five decades, a remarkable journey through the changing fortunes of the entertainment industry, family life and the demands of public recognition.

Together, they raised six children: five sons and a daughter,  and built a family that has remained connected to the creative industry.

Two of his sons, Linc Edochie and Yul Edochie, followed his footsteps into acting, while his name and influence continued to attract public interest through the next generation.

For many Nigerians, the image of Pete Edochie as a father was reinforced by the roles he played on screen. He often portrayed the uncompromising family head whose decisions could shape the destiny of his children, the man whose word was law and whose approval was fiercely sought.

Yet, like every family, the Edochies had their own private experiences, triumphs, disagreements and challenges beyond the public gaze.

In recent years, the veteran actor occasionally found himself in the headlines over family issues, particularly controversies surrounding his son Yul’s marital life. Even then, his public comments attracted attention because Nigerians were accustomed to seeing him as a voice of authority and restraint.

His family remained an important part of his life, and his legacy as a father would continue through his children and grandchildren.

Award and recognition

Edochie’s contributions to Nigerian entertainment did not go unnoticed. In 2003, he was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) by the Federal Government, in recognition of his contribution to the nation’s cultural and creative landscape.

He also received the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards, alongside other recognitions celebrating his longevity, artistry and impact on African cinema.

His honours included lifetime achievement recognition and awards celebrating his status as one of the continent’s most influential film figures.

But perhaps the most significant recognition he received was not a trophy, plaque or national honour. It was the respect he commanded across the industry—from actors who grew up watching him to directors, producers, filmmakers, and audiences who regarded him as one of Nollywood’s enduring institutions.

He belonged to a generation that built the industry through long hours, imperfect productions, limited resources and an unshakeable belief in the power of Nigerian stories.

A legend who never stopped being relevant

One of the remarkable things about Pete Edochie’s career was his ability to remain relevant in an industry constantly reinventing itself.

As Nollywood moved from VHS tapes to DVDs, cinema releases, streaming platforms and digital productions, he continued to attract roles and audience interest. His appearance in Genevieve Nnaji’s 2018 film Lionheart introduced him to yet another generation of viewers and reminded audiences that his appeal was not confined to the old Nollywood era. In Lionheart, he played Chief Ernest Obiagu, bringing the familiar dignity and authority that audiences associated with him into a contemporary story about business, family and women navigating a male-dominated corporate world.

He also appeared in newer productions, including films that explored modern relationships, family conflicts and the changing dynamics of Nigerian society. Beyond films, his persona remained a steady presence in interviews, online conversations, skits and popular culture. He could trend simply because of a remark, a proverb, an old scene resurfacing or a younger actor paying tribute to his influence.

He did not need to chase every new trend to remain relevant. His legacy had already become a trend of its own.

The final chapter

In the days preceding his death, Edochie remained a subject of public conversation, with renewed attention on a scheduled interview touching on his son Yul’s personal life and the controversies that had followed.

But the news of his death on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, came as a painful reminder that even the most towering figures are mortal.

His family announced that he died in Enugu at 12:30 a.m., following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. The announcement described him as a beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, and asked for prayers as they mourned the loss.

For fans, colleagues and admirers, the news was difficult to reconcile with the image of the imposing man who had spent decades playing characters seemingly untouched by fear, weakness or mortality.

The Iroko had fallen.

And with him went a chapter of Nigerian film history that cannot be replicated.

Pete Edochie may be gone, but the Iroko he planted in the forest of Nigerian cinema is not falling with him. And generations yet unborn will encounter its shade.

US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.

Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "not certain that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year". 

That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.

The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

articles.title: Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
articles.summary:
Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports

Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 21:13

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman expected to travel to the US next month for G-20 in first trip since start of war

This aerial photograph shows a view of the Riyadh skyline on 23 November 2026

Off

Fresh explosions rocked Riyadh on Wednesday as Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.

The Houthis said that both strikes on the ports “resulted in damage” while the Saudi-led coalition acknowledged that a projectile hit the port of Jazan, resulting in minor damage and no casualties.

The port strikes followed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery. Argus Media, which covers commodity markets, said the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal. The Houthis say they bombed Ras Tanura as retaliation for the Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah controlled by the group.

Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and Western officials tell Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side. Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to delivering military support to Saudi Arabia, but with the exception of Syria - which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.

The Crown Prince met US Central Command chief admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE first reported the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.

The US, Saudi Arabia's top military supplier, however has not publicly committed additional support to the kingdom, although it has troops and advisers inside the country.

Iran tensions simmer

Semafor reported on Wednesday that Mohammed bin Salman will travel to the US next month for the G-20 summit in Miami. Diplomats have speculated for months whether the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia would leave the kingdom amid Houthi strikes and the chances of a new US-Israeli attack on Iran.

'Turn on the weapons spigot': Saudi Arabia asks partners for gear to deter Houthis

Read More »

Tensions between the US and Iran have been simmering for months, with the two sides exchanging blows in the Strait of Hormuz and at some land targets. The US has conducted strikes on Iran’s mainland while Tehran has responded with attacks on US military sites in Kuwait and Bahrain.

Iran said on Wednesday that an oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

Brent, the international oil benchmark, was up 2.5 percent on Wednesday, trading at $84 per barrel.

The Trump administration says that it is not interested in resuming the war on Iran for now, and instead wants to use economic means to collapse the government, mainly through a blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran has been hit by debilitating inflation, although regional officials who have traveled to the capital have reported busy restaurants and a sense of calm. Fars said on Wednesday that a substantial shipment of dollar banknotes had entered Iran from a neighbouring country.

Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem on Wednesday demanded the immediate release of five men identified as members of the Lebanese movement and accused of forming an armed cell.

Speaking in a televised address broadcast by Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel, Qassem said the men had "done nothing wrong" and "must be released immediately".

Security forces had detained the five earlier this month in a mountainous area in northern Lebanon, a predominantly Christian region far from Hezbollah's main strongholds.

A judge on Wednesday ordered their continued detention pending investigation, a judicial source told AFP.

"We are being patient in order to preserve civil peace, but patience in the face of injustice has limits," Qassem warned, adding the group would "push back against danger" if necessary.

The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

In May, the Israeli defence ministry said that the two sides had begun formal talks to replace the current memorandum, with discussions focusing on joint investment in research, development and weapons production.

The suggested framework was to move the relationship from aid to a more reciprocal partnership. 

The Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan research body that advises the US Congress, further confirmed this in a June report that US and Israeli officials were discussing a possible shift after 2028 away from direct military aid and towards joint programmes.

Israel, a full-scale partner

In July, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives narrowly passed a $1.5 trillion budget for the US Department of War, and the bill included a controversial provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Netanyahu put it - turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner. 

Future presidents would not be able to simply withdraw from such a project. 

Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall

Read More »

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is must-pass legislation, as it is needed to fund all of the Pentagon's operations in the year to come. The Senate will have to consider it soon.

But emboldened by the incoming Democratic majority in January, a dozen Democrats, led by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, are seeking to remove the provisions related to Section 219, which establishes the "United States–Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative".

The project would identify jointly developed or Israeli-origin technologies for potential integration into US systems; ensure collaborative research initiatives involving government, private sector and academic institutions in both countries protect "sensitive technology"; and ultimately align military efforts with the Department of War that include the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Missile Defense Agency and the United States Space Command, among others. 

Huckabee said at the Institute for National Security Studies conference on Tuesday that American lives are saved "every day" because "we pick up intelligence from our partners in Israel". 

Military ties continue

On 3 November, Trump said that his administration will not give its yearly military aid to Israel starting next year, because of a prior understanding he made with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. 

Trump added that weapon sales and other forms of military cooperation would continue. 

Speaking on Fox News, the president said that the two had agreed months ago to end the military aid since Israel no longer needed it.

Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy

Read More »

“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump said.

“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he added.

Trump said Israel would be able to purchase weapons from the United States and other countries, suggesting that the change would affect the form of assistance rather than bring an end to military ties.

"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," he said.

The comments came as Republican lawmakers and establishment Democrats running for Congress - as well as hundreds of statewide races - faced growing electoral pressure over support for Israel ahead of the midterm elections.

And indeed, the so-called blue tsunami, led by an energised progressive Democratic movement that wants to curb US aid to Israel, washed over Capitol Hill and state legislatures, including several governorships.
