articles.title: Expert reaction: what the Timms review into Pip disability benefits gets right – and where it falls short
articles.summary:
Zamrznuti tonovi/Shutterstock

Personal independence payments (Pip) are welfare benefits that are meant to help people with long-term health issues cope with the extra costs associated with their conditions. But it’s controversial – from the application process to who qualifies.

Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, has published a long-awaited report into Pip, recommending a raft of changes to the system.

Here’s what experts made of his findings.

‘Constant dread’ during the application process

Stephanie Allan, Research Associate in Mental Health & Wellbeing, University of Glasgow

Humanising the benefits system, as Timms claims his review will, is crucial. As part of our research, participants told us that applying and being assessed for disability benefits such as Pip has caused psychological distress, particularly for those applying due to conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder or schizophrenia.

We’ve been told assessments can feel like “being on trial”, with constant dread of unexpected letters coming through the door, and can even cause re-traumatisation.

The review’s call to reduce unnecessary reviews and improve communication between assessors and applicants may address these issues – as may its suggestion of training assessors in trauma-informed practice. This means they should offer consistency and transparency in explaining how decisions are made and not minimising people’s difficulties.

Some people living with serious mental health problems face profound challenges and struggle to do things many people take for granted. The report proposes fast-tracked paths for peopel who have “serious, well-evidenced conditions whose impact on their daily life is clear”. But it’s ambiguous which conditions this will cover, and this could also cause worry for potential Pip recipients.

While the Timms review acknowledges the impact of stigma, our work emphasises how negative media reporting and politicians’ speeches about disability benefits can cause distress, especially if it frames claimants as burdens. It can also influence how people respond, and make them even more afraid to participate in society.

People with fluctuating mental health problems have told us that fears of being falsely reported for fraud by neighbours and community members can make them avoid activities such as volunteering, exercise, or even taking part in clinical research that could improve mental health for them or others in future.

Training on trauma-informed care is arguably not enough on its own. Without stronger legal safeguards – such as independent oversight when things go wrong – the power imbalance between claimants and those in charge remains intact.

Furthermore, reforming the claiming process by itself will not make people feel safe if political rhetoric and media narratives continue to frame disabled people as a burden.

Every day is different when you’re disabled

Steve Atkin-Teillet, Lecturer in Law, Nottingham Law School

The nature of some conditions means that symptoms can fluctuate from day to day. The review found that in order to capture the varying nature of a claimant’s needs, the Pip application form should be changed so that it’s simpler for claimants to report what they experience.

This should be underpinned by better training for Pip assessors on the rules surrounding variances and fluctuations in what someone is able to do. This should not only include a requirement to assess whether someone can perform an activity, but also whether they can do so reliably.

Stephen Timms’ report claims it will ‘humanise the benefits system’
House of Commons/Flickr, CC BY

Right now, a claimant should only be considered capable of a task if they can do it safely, repeatedly and in a reasonable amount of time. In 2024, I recommended that the new Pip form include these three elements under each activity the claimant describes, as well as on the government’s Pip advice page.

At present, people claiming Pip can be assessed by any type of medical professional. Someone applying for mental health reasons could be given a physiotherapist as their assessor. This is a concern, as claimants sometimes feel their assessor was not competent or well placed to understand their condition.

The Timms review proposes a specific Pip assessor role – but this doesn’t fully address concerns over competency. As it stands, it’s unclear how someone in this new role would be trained to assess a full range of potential disabilities and conditions.

More understanding of neurodiversity since Pip launched

Mindy Ptolomey, Lecturer in Disability Studies, University of Leeds

The review has highlighted that when Pip was designed and implemented – back in 2012 under David Cameron’s coalition government – it did not consider the barriers neurodivergent people face in everyday life. Neither did it take into account their needs in terms of the application process. As pointed out in the interim report of the review, long paper forms with no online version, rigid deadlines, and having to use the phone can all create barriers for neurodivergent people.

Read more:
The Milburn report sets out a plan to improve the lives of young people who are Neet – experts respond

The review’s recognition of neurodivergent people’s needs is especially important as the diagnosis of ADHD and autism has increased in recent years. In the UK, new adult autism diagnoses increased more than tenfold from 2010 to 2023, and monthly referrals for ADHD diagnosis more than tripled between 2019 and 2024.

A government review published last month highlights that there is no evidence of widespread over-diagnosis. These increases are instead due to a range of factors like historical under-recognition and greater awareness.

It’s encouraging to see a continued commitment to involving disabled people during the design and implementation stages of any reforms. Disabled people were part of the review’s steering group and their views were included in a range of ways. However, more can be done to make sure the people who face the greatest barriers are included in shaping reforms. Involving neurodivergent people is important for ensuring the core purposes of Pip are delivered supporting disabled people’s independence, participation and autonomy.

Pip can make an important contribution to meeting the additional costs of being disabled, for those in and out of work. The review recommends linking the amount people will receive through Pip more closely to the additional costs they face due to disability or health conditions.

However, questions remain about how these costs will be identified and calculated. Previous data shows that it is difficult for disabled people to understand the additional costs of being disabled, especially when you’ve had a condition all your life, which is the case for neurodivergent people.

Mental health conditions could face cuts

Sarah Ledden, Research Associate in Population Mental Health, King’s College London

One key element of the proposed reforms is to only provide Pip to those who incur additional costs due to a long-term health condition or disability. The challenge here will be creating appropriate mechanisms to assess these costs, without repeating current difficulties the system has in evaluating fluctuating and ‘harder-to-see’ conditions.

The Department for Work and Pensions recently released a research report which aimed to understand the disability-related needs that create additional living costs among Pip recipients. It indicated that people with mental health conditions were less likely to have additional costs for equipment and travel needs, though they did more often have paid treatment needs (such as counselling).

However, these people experience employment and income gaps, earning 32% less than people with no such conditions, and higher levels of financial hardship. This indicates that there are often financial challenges for people with mental health conditions, but many of these costs may be hidden or cumulative.

If the transition to a new benefit is managed poorly, with proposed impact assessments not designed to capture these types of costs, it risks people with mental health conditions being left behind. The Timms review has recommendations around understanding inequalities in experiences and outcomes of different groups, which will be vital in ensuring the system works.

The DWP’s evidence published with the review reported that only 1 in 5 Pip claimants reported having a single condition. Most people reported multiple conditions. Only 4.4% of total Pip claims are those solely claiming for depression and anxiety, with these more often reported alongside other conditions.

The rise in these cases is based on the “primary condition” reported on Pip claims, although this is in line with evidence that these conditions are rising in the general population.

Previous research from our team on Pip receipt among people who accessed specialist mental healthcare found that receiving Pip is related to greater clinical need (including diagnosis type and longer time receiving care). If the government aims to reduce welfare spending by assessing mental health Pip claims using stricter criteria, this may not have as big an impact as they expect.

This article was corrected on November 27 to remove a reference to Pip being a UK-wide benefit. In Scotland it was replaced with adult disability payment in 2025.

Stephanie Allan currently receives funding from the Chief Scientist Office at the University of Glasgow.

Mindy Ptolomey has previously received funding from the Economic Social Research Council and the British Academy.

Sarah Ledden and Steve Atkin-Teillet do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Indonesia’s huge peat fires burn underground – so we still don’t know just how much carbon they have released
articles.summary:
A recent peatland forest fire in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, one of thousands across the country this year. Amazing Aerial / shutterstock

At the peak of Indonesia’s 2026 wildfire season, we were in Palangka Raya, a city of 300,000 people surrounded by dense peatland rainforest. Smoke covered the city in a thick yellow haze. Between mid-September and mid-October, we recorded air pollution levels equivalent to smoking about 14 cigarettes per day. On the worst days, that rose to around 30.

Our colleague Sanz Rio Griffio Limin is from the region and works at Cimtrop, a peatland research centre at the local university. “This year the fires are the worst in my lifetime,” he told us. “I am 41, and I have never seen this kind of smoke and fires.”

Unlike most wildfires, peatland fires burn beneath the ground as well as above it. These underground fires can smoulder for weeks or months and are notoriously difficult to extinguish.

Peat has accumulated carbon from dead plants over thousands of years. When it burns, that carbon is released into the atmosphere. The deeper the fire burns, the more carbon it releases.

Indonesia has wildfires every year, but they’re significantly more intense in El Niño years like this one, when there is less rain and the ground dries out further.

The country last experienced wildfires on this scale in 2015, another El Niño year. In September and October that year, Indonesia’s peat fires were releasing carbon dioxide faster than the entire European Union.

But estimates of emissions from these fires remain uncertain because we have surprisingly few direct measurements of how deeply the peat burns. That’s why one of us (Maria) travelled to Palangka Raya to join an international team of researchers measuring how much peat these fires consume and how much carbon they emit, alongside colleagues at Cimtrop, where our co-author Kitso is based.

Measuring the hidden fires

Burning peat has a particularly intense smell, which penetrated even through our face masks and other protective gear. That smell, and the wall of heat and smoke, would hit us the moment we arrived and stepped out of an air-conditioned car.

We had to be constantly vigilant for unseen underground fires and the risk of falling into a peat fire pit. Surface fires would sometimes spontaneously ignite within a few feet of our team.

Researchers at a recently burned site measuring soil moisture and density, water table depth and peat burn depth.
PEAKFire

The scale of the burning was extraordinary. Reaching some sites meant driving for up to 45 minutes along narrow clay tracks through an almost post-apocalyptic landscape. At the sites, fires had consumed peat underground, burning away tree roots and causing them to collapse.

Previous research suggests the water level needs to remain within about 40 centimetres of the peat surface to reduce fire risk. This year, we measured water tables between 2 and 4 metres below the surface – leaving huge layers of dry peat available to burn.

Across ten sites, we used drones and ground surveys to measure how deeply the peat had burned and estimate how much had been consumed by fire. We also collected soil samples and recorded greenhouse gas emissions from burned and unburned peat. At active fires, we measured gases released by smouldering peat, including carbon dioxide and methane, and invisible but toxic air pollution particles.

Why it matters

The impacts of Indonesian peat fires extend far beyond areas that burn. Smoke is transported across borders, affecting millions of people across south-east Asia, disrupting daily life and causing widespread health problems. In years like 2015 or 2026, Indonesia’s peat fires are also one of the largest sources of carbon emitted into the atmosphere, anywhere in the world.

This fire burned the top 40cm or so of peat. In a fire like this, burning peat will emit far more carbon than surface vegetation.
Kitso Kusin

However, estimates remain uncertain because we still don’t fully understand how burn depth and emissions vary under different peat conditions. Measurements from our fieldwork this year will help improve these estimates and strengthen smoke forecasting systems in Indonesia and surrounding countries.

We also helped local researchers deploy an additional 25 low-cost air pollution particle sensors to track smoke exposure across urban and rural areas close to peatland environments during future fire seasons.

The peat fires and haze crisis in Indonesia are largely a human-made disaster caused by peatlands being drained and degraded, making them more vulnerable to fires during droughts. Restoration can reduce this risk by raising the water table and rewetting the peat, for example, through wells or by blocking drainage canals.

These measures can reduce the number of fires. However, restoration cannot fully restore the fire resistance of intact peatlands. Protecting remaining intact peatlands while restoring those that have already been drained and degraded is our best opportunity to reduce future fire risk, protect communities from hazardous smoke and preserve globally important carbon stores.

Ailish Graham receives funding from UK Research and Innovation.
This work was funded by a NERC Urgency Grant, it brought together a team from CIMTROP, University of Palangka Raya, London School of Economics, Liverpool John Moores University and University of Leeds.

Kitso Kusin works for the organization (university).

Maria Nolan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Accurate job descriptions and pay transparency shouldn’t be radical ideas
articles.summary:
Drazen Zigic/Shutterstock

Salary negotiations can feel like a bit of a game, but new UK legislation may change the rules. Under draft government plans, employers will be required to publish the salary range for any job advertised.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a legal requirement for pay transparency in job adverts. There have also been proposals for equal pay reforms for those with disabilities or of an ethnic minority.

However, the Equality and Human Rights Commission is going further. It is urging governments to prevent employers from asking candidates about their existing salaries or expectations.

Recruitment is a game played on a very uneven playing field. Hiring the wrong recruit can be expensive and time consuming. But the toll placed on someone who finds themselves in the wrong job can be deep and enduring, potentially damaging their physical and mental health, work engagement, job satisfaction, and diminishing their confidence in their own abilities.

Employers have traditionally used previous earnings as a benchmark or indication of the salary a candidate would be prepared to accept. It’s also a proxy for their value – assuming that we are all worth what other people have decided to pay us.

From a potential employer’s perspective, a candidate’s high previous salary is understood as a sign of “latent quality”. This means it’s an indication of hidden abilities and skills that might not have been revealed at the interview.

Candidates can, of course, refuse to disclose their salary, but even that comes at a cost. It could give the impression that they are less skilled and have fewer alternative options. Gender stereotypes lead recruiters to believe that men are more comfortable discussing money, so they are viewed with more suspicion if reluctant to disclose their current earnings.

Questions about salary expectations can also be tricky for candidates to manage. Opt too low and you risk being offered a lower starting salary. Too high and you reduce your chances of a job offer. Evidence suggests that a collaborative approach and a precise starting bid seem to serve candidates well in their salary negotiations. For example, asking for £34,575 works better than £35,000.

Making salaries fairer for all

Much of the gender pay gap can be traced back to starting salaries. The explanations for this are complex, but include the anchoring effects of the salaries that recruiters expect to pay. This includes lower initial rates for female candidates, and the salaries that candidates feel able to ask for: men are more likely to negotiate hard when it comes to their starting salary, and employers are more likely to concede to their demands.

A similar story is seen with ethnicity. Certain groups – for example Black candidates and those from south-east and east Asia – seem to come out of negotiations with a worse deal. Racial and gender stereotypes can influence both candidates’ and recruiters’ behaviour.

The gender pay gap can be traced back to women being given lower starting salaries.
fizkes/Shutterstock

The current system of anchoring future salaries to previous salaries perpetuates discrimination, allowing people who hold privilege to cling on to an early advantage throughout their careers. Differences in starting salaries endure for years and it’s estimated that two thirds of the steady-state gender pay gap in the UK – meaning the wage gap that would occur if employment levels were constant and steady, rather than fluctuating as they do now – can be traced back to gender differences in starting salaries.

Furthermore, job adverts are not always an accurate reflection of what the role entails. They’re designed to sell the job to prospective employees. AI-curated job adverts are beginning to sound similar, making it ever harder for a candidate to work out whether they would actually like the job.

Typical AI-generated job adverts are often vague and are full of corporate buzzwords, leaving the potential candidate unsure about what the employer is looking for.

Job descriptions often reflect an idealised account of the role. They are generally written from the perspective of the employer rather than employee. For this reason, they can be light on the day-to-day realities.

Employers might offer interview candidates the chance to ask questions, but this is generally just an extension of the selection process. All parties are aware that this is not the time for an honest conversation.

Experiences vary, but candidates often have little more than a job advert and a single interview to go on. Ultimately this may well backfire for the employer. The organisation might find themselves with the “best” candidate on paper. But if they have missold the job, or misrepresented the organisation, it can lead to unrealistically high employee expectations, lower job satisfaction and a higher chance that their new recruit will quit their job.

“Realistic job previews”, where employers give an honest account of what the job is actually like, have been shown to have a positive impact on employers’ ability to recruit and retain good candidates. Studies have shown that when employees are invited to talk to candidates honestly about the job and the organisation, and are open about the challenges and stresses, potential recruits feel more positive about the integrity of the employer. Their expectations of the role are also more realistic, and they end up performing better and wanting to stay with the new organisation.

Staff turnover is an expensive business. Annual employee turnover across the UK is 34% on average. The cost of replacing each employee earning £25,000 or more is approximately £30,614 for the employer. Any improvements that can be made to the selection process to ensure that new hires are in it for the long haul could reap significant financial rewards.

The plans to increase transparency in salary negotiations feel like a step in the right direction, but providing an accurate description of the job shouldn’t be hailed as a radical approach. Job selection is the start of an ongoing relationship which is bound to be more successful if it starts with more transparency and collaboration.

Julia Yates does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: If politicians really want to cut heating bills they need to trust in green energy – businesses already are
articles.summary:
JustJus/Shutterstock

This year’s United Nations climate summit, Cop31, ended in Antalya without a deal.

It appears that the world’s politicians and policy makers have collectively moved on from building a global coalition against climate change, just as its effects are becoming impossible to ignore.

Yet the public have not stopped worrying. In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.

And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

But perhaps the biggest hurdle to making more climate-friendly changes is the current cost-of-living crisis. It appears to be politically difficult to tell cash-strapped voters to be more environmentally friendly.

Opponents of policies tackling climate change, including British and European right-wing parties and Donald Trump, seem to have effectively persuaded a majority of the public that it is impossible to make climate-friendly choices and keep your bills down. In 2026, 62% of the UK public expected net zero – Britain’s route to climate neutrality – to increase their bills in the short run.

Read more:
Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations

Voters often tend to overestimate how much they would lose from a carbon tax, and to underestimate how much others care.

But despite this, people are starting to notice that climate action cannot be blamed for an economic and environmental crisis fuelled by gas and petrol prices.

The 62% share of voters who think net zero increases their bills is the lowest on record. And 51% expect net zero to be good for the economy in the long run – only 24% think it will hurt it.

Politicians are right to be careful about what voters will accept. French president Emmanuel Macron has learned the hard way, after ten years of public protests, that taxing petrol is unpopular. In Milan, some voters owning polluting cars said they were likely to vote for the far right when the city banned their vehicles from the city centre.

But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.

Cost-of-living crisis is a fossil fuel crisis

In 2021, Russia supplied around 40% of the EU’s pipeline gas imports. Scrambling to replace these imports with liquefied gas from Qatar and the US has sent energy prices through the roof.

Because of its past dependency on Russian fossil fuels, Europe now pays around ten times more than the US for the same quantity of gas. These high prices have hurt the economy and pushed up inflation.

Every unit of electricity generated by wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear power plants cuts consumer bills.

Those resources saved £5.9 billion in gas imports for the UK at the start of the Iran conflict when shipping was blocked through the Strait of Hormuz. Every time no gas is needed to produce electricity, prices come down.

Significant economic damage can be caused by ignoring this. It has been clear for some time now that the future is made of electric cars and batteries. Yet European carmakers still lobby for a perpetual delay of the transition.

This strategy is costing jobs today, having transformed Europe’s leading carmakers into global laggards.

And it also hurts consumers. The world’s cheapest electric cars are made in China. EU efforts to protect what remains of its car industry using tariffs mean they cost consumers 45% more.

Britain has so far avoided the extra cost. But the EU is pushing it to impose similar tariffs.

The largest wind farm in the world opened off the Grimsby coast in 2025.

Business is investing in green energy

But global investors are not as backward-looking as governments. This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence. More than 90% of large-scale renewable investment in 2025 was cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel alternative.

The same self-interested approach could apply to ordinary citizens.

An electric car costs less to run than a petrol one. But delays in the transition mean there are still too few charging points to make it practical for everyone.

Another factor is that in England, for instance, road congestion is taking an increasing toll on the economy, and this primarily affects motorists. Even in the US, where public transport accounts for less than 1% of journeys, when subways are not working, these few passengers switching to the car increase road congestion by 47%.

Pro-car lobbies do try to block investment in walkable cities and public transport. Will they take responsibility for the projected 85% increase in British road congestion by 2040?

Migration is very high on voters’ list of concerns, higher than any other in some British polls. And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries. Without international cooperation on issues like water and energy, the flow of people wanting to escape poverty to live in less affected countries is likely to go up.

We live in an ageing world, and it appears that people are increasingly scared of change. The global mood feels protectionist and as crises accumulate, many want to put their own country first.

Very few environmental activists or politicians seem to speak to these instincts.

But green electricity makes you independent from foreign dictators, global cooperation should make migration more manageable, and many of our current problems come from ignoring climate change, not from trying to address it.

Renaud Foucart does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: We need to talk about young people’s sexual wellbeing – here’s why
articles.summary:
YesPhotographers/Shutterstock.com

Something is changing in Britain’s bedrooms. People in their late teens and early twenties are having sex later and less often than previous generations, and one in three 16- to 24-year-olds now say they have never had sex.

These are among the headline findings from the latest British National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), the once-a-decade study that has tracked the nation’s sex lives since 1990. The latest survey, published across five papers in the Lancet, shows just how much has changed in young people’s sex lives in the last ten years.

At first glance, the headline finding could be seen as good news. Perhaps young people are taking more time before becoming sexually active and making decisions that feel right for them.

Yet alongside changes in sexual activity, Natsal-4 also found that young people had the lowest sexual wellbeing of any age group surveyed. At a time of life when sex is often assumed to be carefree, nearly one in four women aged 16-24, and almost one in five men of the same age, had low sexual wellbeing. Across all participants aged 16-59, the figure was closer to one in seven.

Sexual wellbeing is about much more than whether someone is having sex, or even whether that sex is enjoyable. It is about how people feel about this part of their lives. Do they feel comfortable and confident in themselves? Do they feel respected by others? Can they think or talk about sex without shame or embarrassment? Do they feel able to make choices that are right for them, and get support when they need it?

Sex and relationships are woven into many people’s sense of identity, connection with others, and overall wellbeing. Yet conversations about sex – particularly with young people – often focus on what can go wrong, rather than what helps people feel secure and at ease.

A young person might manage to avoid an unplanned pregnancy or a sexually transmitted infection, but still struggle with feelings of shame about sex. And concerns about sexual wellbeing are not limited to those who are sexually active. Young people who are not having sex may also experience pressures or worries.

The decline in sexual activity may matter less than whether young people feel comfortable and confident about their sex lives.

It’s not easy to say why this decline in sexual activity is happening. Young adults today face major economic pressures: insecure employment, high housing costs and delayed financial independence. There are fewer opportunities to meet and connect with others in-person, while social media and digital technologies have created new sources of social comparison, scrutiny and anxiety.

The COVID pandemic also disrupted a critical period of social and relationship development for many of today’s young people.

In the Natsal-4 survey, people with low sexual wellbeing were more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and depression, and this was particularly the case for men. This relationship almost certainly works in both directions. Poor mental health may make it harder to form or maintain intimate relationships, while worries about sex and intimacy may themselves contribute to emotional distress.

Although we cannot say what causes what, the findings reinforce a simple point: if we care about mental wellbeing, we need to care about sexual wellbeing too, as the evidence shows the two are so intimately intertwined.

COVID also disrupted young people’s relationships.
Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Different for women and men

Low sexual wellbeing is not experienced in the same way by everyone. While overall levels of low sexual wellbeing were similar in men and women of all age groups (one in seven), the patterns underlying them differed in important ways.

Women were more likely than men to report having someone they could talk to openly about their sex life. At the same time, they were more likely to report being upset with others about past sexual experiences.

Men, meanwhile, were more likely to report having a pleasurable sex life, but also more likely to feel shame about some of their thoughts and desires.

These differences reflect the distinct social pressures and expectations that continue to shape women’s and men’s experiences of sex and relationships. They also suggest that improving sexual wellbeing is unlikely to be as simple as increasing knowledge. It may also require enabling people to talk openly about insecurities and expectations in their sexual lives.

For years, public discussions about young people’s sexual lives have focused on whether they are having sex, at what age and how often. The latest Natsal findings suggest that we need to pay attention not only to what they do, but also to how they feel. For many young people, sexual wellbeing remains an overlooked part of the picture. It is time to start talking about it.

Correction: “males” and “females” has been changed to “men” and “women” to accurately reflect the terminology used in the survey.

Kirstin Mitchell receives funding from Scottish Government to research and embed sexual wellbeing in sexual health services nationally. The Natsal-4 study was funded by a grant from the Wellcome Trust with contributions from the UK ESRC and UK NIHR. Kirstin has received speaker fees from the College of Sexual and Relationships Therapists and travel reimbursement from the College of Sexual and Reproductive Health to talk on sexual wellbeing. In 2026, after the submission of the Natsal sexual wellbeing paper, Kirstin was an unpaid contributor to an educational series hosted by Reckitt (manufacturer of Durex condoms).

Ruth Lewis receives funding from Scottish Government to research and embed sexual wellbeing in sexual health services nationally.

articles.title: Strength training can help preserve muscle while using weight-loss drugs, research shows
articles.summary:
Zamrznuti tonovi/ Shutterstock

Weight-loss drugs are helping people to lose substantial amounts of weight and improve their health. However, this weight and body fat loss can also be accompanied by a loss of muscle and strength.

A new landmark study now shows that doing strength training while taking weight loss drugs can help.

Weight-loss drugs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy can have substantial health benefits. Alongside large reductions in body weight and body fat, they can also help people who are overweight and have heart disease to improve blood pressure, blood glucose and blood cholesterol levels, and lower the risk of having a heart attack or stroke.

However, as these drugs become more widely used, it’s important to consider whether solving one health problem could contribute to another.

The weight lost when taking these drugs includes some lean tissue – including muscle. There are several reasons for this.

Weight-loss drugs work by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake. When food intake falls, the body adapts to having fewer resources available and slows the production of new muscle.

Eating less food often means you’re consuming less protein overall. This means your body has less supply of the essential building blocks it needs to make new muscle. As body weight falls, every day movements place less load on the muscles which reduces the stimulus needed to maintain them.

Together, all of this leads to muscle loss. And this loss of muscle may have consequences for strength and independence.

Muscle strength helps you do everyday activities such as climbing the stairs, carrying shopping, getting out of a chair and steadying your body during a stumble.

The concern with weight-loss treatment is that substantial losses of muscle and strength could take people closer to a threshold below which they struggle to function independently and are at an increased risk of falls. This is of particular concern for older adults, since people already naturally tend to lose muscle and strength as we age.

Maintaining muscle

This recent trial involved 120 adults in Australia aged 50-70 years who were overweight or obese and did not exercise often. Everyone received the weight loss drug therapy (specifically tirzepatide – also known as Mounjaro) for 40 weeks.

The researchers then randomly assigned participants to either carry on with their usual levels of activity or do three strength training sessions each week. The training progressed slowly. Participants started with lighter exercises to learn the safe movements before increasing the challenge of performing each exercise. The sessions were also supervised by a qualified clinical exercise physiologist.

Both groups lost a large amount of weight (about 22kg on average) and body fat (about 17kg) during the 40-week period. They also saw similar improvements in their blood pressure, blood glucose and blood cholesterol levels.

The strength training group lost less muscle and built strength.
New Africa/ Shutterstock

Both groups lost some lean soft tissue (including muscle) but strength training offset some of this. The non-strength training group lost 4.7kg of lean tissue, while the strength training group only lost 3.6kg.

Strength was tested in both groups. The test involved straightening the knee against resistance (a knee extension exercise). People who just continued their normal activities could lift about 4kg less by the end of the study. But those who did the strength training throughout could lift 6kg more. The same pattern was found for two tests of upper body strength.

So despite losing some muscle, the exercise group got much stronger.

No specific dietary advice was given to the groups, other than to maintain protein intake. So this effect appears to be wholly down to the strength training.

The improvement in strength is probably explained by the strength training both preserving the amount of muscle and at the same time improving the quality of that muscle.

Strength training and weight loss

The study shows that doing strength training while taking a weight-loss drug can help people maintain muscle and improve strength.

For those who want to give strength training a try, aim to do two or three strength-focused sessions each week. Start with a light or moderate effort and build up gradually.

In the study, the first eight weeks were spent developing the correct technique and getting accustomed to exercise before the difficulty was gradually increased. Follow that principle by starting with manageable body weight exercises or using light resistance bands.

Build towards doing two sets of eight to 12 repetitions of each exercise, where the final couple of repetitions feel challenging. You should aim to do eight to ten different exercises in each session. Try to include lower body exercises (such as a body weight squat or a calf raise) and upper body exercises (such as a wall push up or a lat pull down using a resistance band). If eight to ten exercises per session feels daunting, then it’s fine to start with four to six exercises and build up over time. Be sure to pick exercises you enjoy doing.

As you get more confident and body weight exercises start to feel easier, you can gradually add more resistance. Just remember to keep good technique.

Strength training can help you maintain the muscle strength you need to move well and stay independent throughout ageing. These new findings further highlight the benefit it can have during weight-loss treatment by protecting muscle.

articles.title: Can the International Criminal Court survive Trump’s attacks – and hold world leaders to account?
articles.summary:
More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague.

Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs.

The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution.

“Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast.

The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries.

McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals.

In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says.

The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure.

Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court.

“The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it.

Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC.

While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says:

There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states.

Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall.

Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date.

So will the ICC survive?

McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order.

“I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says.

McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order:

It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers.

Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC.

I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court.

Disclosure statement

Carrie McDougall does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Sound mixing is by Michelle Macklem, and our theme music is by Neeta Sarl. Ashylnne McGhee is head of editorial innovation. Gemma Ware is head of audio at The Conversation UK. Misha Ketchell and Stephen Khan are our editors-in-chief.

articles.title: Is Russia about to launch a nuclear weapon into Earth’s orbit? A space law expert explains the threat
articles.summary:
Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Images

As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports.

If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation, albeit without giving any potential launch window.

These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow.

Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems.

Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial, it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”.

What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite?

A lesson on cooperation

The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia.

During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”.

A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to:

place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere.

Read more:
Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it

A nuclear ‘aurora’

No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth.

One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “aurora”. One eyewitness, then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”.

The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime.

The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities.

Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage.

The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu.
Capnez/Wikimedia

What happens in space is a threat on Earth

Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit.

These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “space citizens”.

Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”.

During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance.

Mitigating the threat through verification

So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space?

As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition.

The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument.

Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report, they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”.

The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections.

In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch.

As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise, we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968.

The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations.

The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk.

In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space.

Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too.

Art Cotterell's postdoctoral fellowship is co-funded by the UNSW Nuclear Innovation Centre and UNSW Law & Justice. He is affiliated with the Australasian Centre for Space Governance.

articles.title: Using AI to hunt for Black Friday bargains? That ‘great deal’ might not exist
articles.summary:
The Conversation, CC BY-SA

To get the most out of Black Friday sales, a bit of research is always useful. Ideally, this involves working out what you might want to buy – and checking prices – before sales begin.

Once the sales are under way, comparing prices, delivery costs and delivery times at different stores can feel onerous and time-consuming, especially if you’re worried you might miss out on a deal.

To streamline their search for a bargain, some shoppers are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to do the research for them.

Can AI really help you snag a deal? The answer is yes, maybe. But there are reasons to proceed carefully.

Sending bots on a bargain hunt

AI is being used to take the legwork out of all sorts of tasks. It makes sense consumers across the world are increasingly putting it to work as a shopping companion.

Say you’re looking for a new coffee machine or laptop this Black Friday. Rather than trawl through dozens of different sites yourself, you might ask a tool such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to search the web for you and prepare a spreadsheet with a list of options.

A recent survey by the Australian Retail Council and market research firm Roy Morgan found this Black Friday, one in four respondents were planning to use an AI chatbot for research.

Among this group, 72% said it would be their first time doing so. If you fall into this category, there are a few things to be aware of as you check any recommendations.

Bogus bargains, ‘ghost stores’ and ads

Hallucination is a well-known feature of generative AI tools. In the context of shopping with AI, this means some products, prices and stores may be entirely made up or misinterpreted.

A related concern is whether AI tools can reliably distinguish between genuine online stores and the fake or “ghost stores” that spring up online during sales periods.

Then, of course, there’s advertising.

Many AI tools, including the free and low-cost versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Search’s AI Overview and AI Mode, have already started rolling out advertising.

Both OpenAI and Google say advertisements shown to users are clearly labelled. But depending on your settings, the ads you see may be informed by your previous conversations with these tools.

Other generative AI tools don’t have ads. Anthropic, for example, has pledged to keep Claude ad-free. And Google’s Gemini app remains free of advertising, at least for now.

The other side of the checkout

Even if you decide not to use AI this Black Friday, it could still shape the deals you see. Some retailers are reportedly already using AI to guide their discounting strategies.

AI is already changing the way companies decide what discounts to offer to everyone.
Ashkan Forouzani/Unsplash

This includes using sophisticated models and past sales data to work out the smallest discount they need to offer to sell a product.

Another potential headwind for shoppers is the use of AI by retailers to personalise prices to the amount a consumer is likely to be prepared to pay, sometimes called “surveillance pricing”.

Currently, this is not explicitly against the law unless the surveillance pricing involves discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, sex or disability.

Read more:
AI is using your data to set personalised prices online. It could seriously backfire

Handing over your wallet

By Black Friday next year, new tools which go beyond simple research may be more commonplace: AI shopping agents. These tools can find stores selling what you’re looking for, compare prices and then complete the purchase on your behalf.

For example, Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in Australia last week, integrates with existing social media accounts and can complete tasks on your behalf.

Other tech companies are also venturing into the space. OpenAI recently launched its Dots agent, and Google’s offerings include Agentic Checkout and Gemini Tasks. Amazon offers its own shopping agent but blocks other third-party agents from accessing its site.

Can we make agents safe?

Developers such as Meta say they are building in protections to prevent consumer AI agents “going rogue” and overstepping their authority or spending instructions.

But even with safeguards in place, other risks could be amplified. AI agents rely on “context” to execute the purchases their consumers are likely to prefer. Essentially, this means information about your previous interactions is used to predict what you might want in the future.

More broadly, there is the risk AI tools may not be working in shoppers’ best interests. An OECD paper this month warned commercial partnerships could shape which products and prices AI tools recommend, in ways that may not be understood by shoppers.

The federal government has flagged new laws may be needed to respond to the rise of AI shopping agents, including to guard against manipulation or exploitative personalised pricing.

Some old-fashioned common sense

So, what’s the advice? By all means, use AI to find a Black Friday bargain, if you choose. But be sceptical. Treat its recommendations as just one piece of information.

It is worth checking the policies of your preferred AI tool to see if you can turn off its memory of earlier chats.

You may also be able to limit advertising and prevent your prompts from being used for training.

Ultimately, getting the best deal still means weighing up your options, sticking to a budget and thinking about whether you really need what’s on sale.

Jeannie Marie Paterson receives funding from the Austrlian Research Council and the Medical Research Future Fund.

articles.title: 50 years of the Sex Pistols: not agents of chaos, but dreamers of a utopia
articles.summary:
John Mead/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images

On November 26 1976, a London-based punk band released a record that created shock waves around the world.

While not the first punk single to be released (The Damned’s New Rose, Radio Birdman’s Burn my Eye EP, and I’m Stranded by the Saints were released a few weeks earlier), Anarchy in the UK, by the Sex Pistols set the tone and a high bar for what was to follow.

With its snarling lyrics (“I am an antichrist”) and raw sound, the song blew a gaping hole in 1970s complacency.

The Sex Pistols are often thought to be obnoxious anarchists who promoted chaos. But in many ways they were the opposite.

Here are five ways they created a template for a more inclusive, more tolerant, and better balanced society that remains relevant in today’s uncertain world.

1. Social and political convention

Like many parts of the developed world, Britain in the mid-1970s faced economic decline, industrial unrest and growing disillusionment with established institutions.

Anarchy in the UK, followed by the band’s next single, God Save the Queen, released during Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee in 1977, voiced the anger and alienation of many people while raising questions about national authority and identity.

The Pistols opened a door for many young people, inviting them to challenge established regimes, and to say no.

Their assertion that there was “no future” is also relevant today.

2. Style and fashion

Alongside their strong influence on music, the Pistols heavily influenced style and fashion.

It is sometimes claimed the Pistols were conceived as a vehicle for Vivienne Westwood’s iconic clothing, which included bondage wear. As well as wearing her clothes, the band also took their name from her shop SEX on Chelsea’s Kings Road in London.

Westwood’s punk stylings encouraged others to create distinctive clothes and outfits from everyday and discarded items, including bin-bags and safety pins.

Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren and Viviane Westwood outside Bow Street Magistrate Court, after being remanded on bail for fighting in 1977.
Daily Mirror/Bill Kennedy/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images

Based on her work with the Sex Pistols, and their manager Malcolm McLaren, Westwood’s career as a fashion iconoclast continued until her death in 2022.

Elsewhere, graphic designer Jamie Reid’s combination of “ransom note” typography and situationist style détournement has had a lasting effect on graphic art and design, while the filmic work of Julien Temple (who made the Sex Pistols 1980 film The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle) has heavily influenced the development of the rock biopic.

3. DIY

One of the Pistols main influences was in the emergence of a DIY approach to music.

This is perhaps epitomised in the Pistols infamous gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4 1976, which inspired attendees to form their own bands (famously: Joy Division, Buzzcocks and The Smiths).

The Sex Pistols perform at the Lesser Free Trade Hall, Manchester, June 4 1976.
Paul Welsh/Redferns via Getty Images.

In this, the myth that the Pistols “couldn’t play” simply inspired the realisation that anyone could pick up a guitar and make a record.

This DIY approach also involved the dissemination and promotion of music and the artists, through home-made fanzines, the precursor to the blogs and zines that proliferate today.

4. Gender and inclusivity

The Pistols encouraged women to become musicians.

Siouxsie Sioux was a member of the Pistols entourage, the Bromley Contingent, contributing to the chaos of the Sex Pistols’ infamous TV confrontation with Bill Grundy before founding the Banshees.

Palmolive and Viv Albertine of the Slits were previously members of the (unrecorded) Flowers of Romance along with John Ritchie (aka Sid Vicious). Chrissie Hynde, who had worked at SEX, went on to form The Pretenders. Poly Styrene was inspired to form X-Ray Spex having seen an early Pistols gig in Hastings in 1975.

The Pistols were central to a London punk scene that embraced and promoted diversity and difference at a time of racial tensions and intolerance.

5. Global influence

The Pistols soon found fans across the world, including in many countries in the Soviet orbit, where their anti-establishment pronouncements found a resonance among disaffected youth.

In Indonesia, the circulation of semi-legal cassette tapes, and the few music publications tolerated by President Suharto’s “New Order” ultimately inspired an anarcho punk scene typified by Bandung band Runtah.

Thriving punk scenes have developed across the globe from Brazil to Japan, from Australia to the Arctic.

At a downtown bar in Perth, Australia, decades after the Sex Pistols first performed, another punk band rattle through their electrifying and energetic set to an adoring and enthusiastic audience. Pogoing may have evolved into moshing, but otherwise much remains the same.

Amyl and the Sniffers are among the latest in a long line of bands from around the world to have embraced the spirit of punk and the Pistols, carrying the legacy to a new generation of audiences.

This article draws on The Routledge Handbook of the Sex Pistols, edited by the authors with Mike Dines and Gabriela Gelain.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
articles.summary:
Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.

These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.

Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed in the war — and potentially as many as 700,000.

For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.

The international dimension

Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.

Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production, outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence.

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy, economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a rapid victory over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.

That support has taken many forms. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.

Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

Targeting support

In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition, it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium. In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.

For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.

The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent.

Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws. The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine.

Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties.

Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant.

Read more:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s removal of two top defence officials highlights the role of morale in long wars

Attacking the secure ‘rear’

In military terms, the rear is the area furthest from the enemy and ideally secure from military threat. For both Ukraine and Russia, this area has been other countries.

While Russia and Ukraine cannot attack the assets of other countries directly, they can and do engage in espionage against other countries.

For Russia, these efforts have focused on destabilizing Europe using drones and other assets via attacks that that are easily deniable. Russia also seeks to create pressure through violating European air space. The more Russia destabilizes Europe, Ukraine’s primary ally, the better its chances in the conflict.

For Ukraine, Russia’s aspirations to be a so-called Great Power mean its network is global — so Ukrainian special operation forces and intelligence agencies strike at Russian assets abroad where possible. These range from attacks in nearby areas, like the Baltics, to Africa and beyond.

Read more:
Putin wanted to make Russia great again. Instead, Ukraine is the new rising power in Europe

While news agencies view this development as widening the conflict, and the United Nations may wish to prevent the conflict from going global, the reality is it’s been a global conflict since before 2022.

The strikes in Libya and the Baltic, and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediate acknowledgement of Ukraine’s role, is just making it public.

James Horncastle does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Climate diplomacy is stuck – these three big changes would get it moving again
articles.summary:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, held in Antalya, Turkey, was being branded “possibly the worst Cop in history” even before its sorry conclusion.

I was there, and the conference was badly managed from start to finish: initial traffic jams and queues sapped energy and goodwill, while the final plenary was one embarrassment after another, with the summit president sniping at the UN’s climate chief (to audible gasps from delegates), and the closing “Antalya pact” being comprehensively rejected.

This sad outcome was not merely the fault of the conference’s Turkish-Australian presidency, however. The bigger issue is that climate diplomacy is stuck – and has been for several years. Structural changes are required, three in particular.

1. Climate finance is not an optional extra

First, climate finance – money provided to developing countries to help them tackle climate change – has to be increased, in particular public, grant-based finance from developed states.

This may seem an odd place to start for those weaned on the mainstream western media, where most accounts of Cop31’s failure focused on the stand off over fossil fuels. But climate finance is not an optional extra under the Paris agreement: it is the glue that holds the entire arrangement together. Ensuring adequate finance flows is one of the agreement’s three main stated aims (alongside limiting global temperature rises and supporting adaptation). And these flows are meant to progressively increase in line with mitigation ambitions and adaptation needs.

But in recent years they have not. At Cop29 in Baku, an ambitious new finance goal was planned. But instead, the conference saw a pushed-through decision that failed to offer the “progression beyond previous efforts” required by Paris and drew widespread condemnation from developing states. Nigeria termed the deal “an insult” to the UN Climate Convention.

Actual country pledges and disbursements have been falling short too. This year has seen a 70% drop in total developed country finance pledges. Meanwhile, the UK is cutting its development assistance to 0.3% of gross national income, while halving its climate finance.

The consequences have been profound. By no coincidence, within a year of the finance debacle in Baku the other side of the global climate bargain had unravelled too. The 2025 round of national mitigation plans were barely more ambitious than their previous iterations, mostly late, and collectively non-compliant with the goals of the Paris agreement.

For many developing countries, inadequate climate finance was one of the biggest frustrations at Cop31.
Rehman Asad / Shutterstock

Cop31 continued this pattern. On the conference’s eve, EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra declared the prospects for additional climate finance “dead in the water”. New developed world pledges for the Adaptation Fund, which helps countries prepare for and cope with the effects of climate change, totalled just US$50 million, less than half the cost of a single F-35 fighter jet.

The predictable result was deadlock on most key negotiation tracks. Indeed, for many developing countries, as well as NGOs, it was above all this climate finance issue – and not the question of whether “fossil fuels” should be named or not – that most underpinned their rejection of the Antalya pact.

The lesson should be clear: to unblock future climate summits, vastly improved finance offerings will be needed from developed countries. And that means that money will have to be diverted from elsewhere, including from the US$2.9 trillion being spent globally on militaries and war.

2. Climate coalitions need to become alliances

More money will not be enough though. Sharper political strategies are also needed, ones that are appropriate to a geopolitically fractured world and to tackling fossil fuel interests.

Cop30 in Belém, Brazil, brought a big step forward on this, with its recognition that “coalitions of the willing” are needed to overcome the UN’s consensus rules. Right now, these rules effectively give fossil fuel-dependent countries a veto on meaningful action. This led to a new process explicitly focused on “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which began with a 57-country summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, in early 2026.

The risk, though, is that such coalitions just become new talking shops, and lack teeth. The “national roadmaps” that countries in the Santa Marta coalition are producing seem to illustrate this: the first wave of published roadmaps contains not a single new major policy commitment.

But other coalitions show us what might be possible. On the greenhouse gas methane (the focus of my current research), a powerful network of international partnerships, NGOs, funders and regulatory initiatives has transformed policy and practice over the last five years.

And building on the EU’s world-leading methane regulation, this coalition is now constructing a global marketplace that rewards cleaner producers with preferential market access, in order to help drive down methane emissions.

To really work, however, both this and other such coalitions will need commitment, regulation and enforcement. Voluntary initiatives will not be enough. And over time, such ad hoc “climate clubs” will need to transform into something much firmer – binding, treaty-based climate alliances.

3. Public pressure and protest matter

Last, it should be stressed that progress in international climate politics is not the responsibility of diplomats alone. Whatever they achieve, or do not, always reflects diverse lobbying and social pressures.

And sadly, on this front there has been a sharp regression. Since a peak in 2020, mass climate activism has largely died out. Media coverage of climate change has declined worldwide. And, spurred on by the Trump administration and war, fossil fuel interests are ascendant.

These things will only be changed through education, mobilisation and a widespread taking to the streets.

As Tasneem Essop, executive director of the NGO Climate Action Network, put it during an early Cop31 press conference: “We cannot give up on multilateralism … But if we can’t win back home, we cannot expect to win things in this space.”

Jan Selby receives funding from the European Research Council. He is a member of the Green Party of England and Wales.

articles.title: The efficiency paradox: why greener AI means more waste
articles.summary:
Data centres are getting bigger and more abundant, not necessarily more efficient. cflaten/Shutterstock

AI is increasingly being promoted as a solution to climate change. It can help companies use less fuel, reduce waste and make production more efficient.

For example, AI can help delivery companies plan more efficient routes, reducing the fuel they use and the emissions they produce. Similar savings could be made across other industries and transport networks, potentially reducing the overall environmental impact. But greater efficiency can also encourage more consumption.

AI is being promoted as a climate solution and as a driver of competitiveness, productivity and economic growth. The World Trade Organization estimates that the widespread adoption of AI could increase global trade by around 40% by 2040. This is generally presented as a benefit.

But there is an obvious contradiction here. If AI makes firms more efficient and profitable, it encourages further investment and expansion. Successful firms do not use productivity gains to produce less, but to expand and to make greater profits.

When these dynamics are generalised across the economy, the result is more production, transportation, resource extraction, consumption and ultimately more environmental destruction.

This is capitalism’s efficiency paradox, known as the Jevons paradox. According to William Stanley Jevons, a 19th-century English economist, any increase in resource efficiency generates an increase in long-term resource consumption, rather than a decrease.

Read more:
DeepSeek claims to have cured AI’s environmental headache. The Jevons paradox suggests it might make things worse

New technologies can help businesses produce more goods using less energy, materials and labour. But by making production cheaper and faster, they can also encourage businesses to make and sell more, increasing the total amount of resources that people use.

Industrial efficiency gains have been a defining feature of capitalism since the Industrial Revolution. Steam-powered textile mills and coal mines in the late 18th century, the Bessemer steel process (making steel by blowing air through molten iron) in the 19th century, and Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th all dramatically increased efficiency.

The industrial revolution has evolved as efficiency improved, from the development of coal mines in the 18th century to Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th century.
Parilov/Shutterstock

Yet none of these efficiency gains reduced society’s overall consumption of resources. Rather, they underpinned successive waves of industrial expansion, fossil-fuel use and environmental degradation.

AI is no different.

My research shows how digital technologies provide a historical example of this dynamic.

For decades, improvements in computers, telecommunications and data storage have allowed companies to spread different stages of production across several countries. They can now use real-time digital networks to share information and coordinate manufacturing and trade around the world.

These technologies have made possible today’s highly integrated global supply chains, allowing firms to source components from thousands of suppliers and move goods across continents with extraordinary speed and precision.

The environmental consequences are immense.

Digital technologies have helped companies produce and sell more goods around the world. This has increased the demand for raw materials, pollution from transport and damage to the natural environment. International trade in goods is now linked to around 30% of threats to the world’s species

Rather than reversing these trends, AI is deepening them. It is making supply chains faster, more responsive and more geographically extensive. From a business perspective, this is progress. Environmentally, it accelerates ecological breakdown.

Cleaner technology, more fossil fuels

The same contradiction can be seen in the energy sector. Much discussion of AI and green technology assumes that cleaner technologies replace dirtier ones. Yet, as the historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz shows, new energy systems tend to accumulate on top of rather than substitute for each other.

Wood, coal, oil, gas and renewables have largely been added to one another rather than replacing one another. Green technologies are making fossil-fuel industries more efficient, rather than replacing them.

Many of the technologies being promoted as climate solutions, including AI, are actually accelerating the extraction of fossil fuels that is driving climate change.

In Guyana, since commercial oil production began in 2019, the country has become one of the world’s fastest-growing producers of oil, with targets to produce 1.3 million barrels per day by 2027. AI-enabled drilling and “geosteering” – the real-time adjustment of a well’s path to keep it within oil-bearing rock – are increasing the rate of oil extraction.
