It’s something we’re all familiar with – the frustration of a bad night’s sleep. But what is a bad night’s sleep, exactly? For some, it might look like lying awake, being unable to fall asleep. For others, sleep may come quickly, only to be interrupted by unwanted early morning wake ups.

Others may find that even with a solid eight hours a night, the struggle to get out of bed in the morning makes the thought of “five more minutes” an irresistible prospect. If only we could start our days with the same vigour we use when hitting the snooze button.

Bad nights are more than just inconvenient. Poor sleep is associated with a suite of negative health outcomes, ranging from cardiovascular disease and diabetes to poor mental health and dementia. And with clinically significant insomnia affecting over 15% of the general adult population, it is unsurprising that insufficient sleep has been branded a public health epidemic.

There is no shortage of opinions on how to get a better night’s sleep. We are also spoilt for choice by the healthtech industry, where a booming gadget market vies for our attention with promises of making sleepless nights a thing of the past. Yet the guidance we receive from these sources tends to be quite generic. And because we each sleep a bit differently, one-size-fits-all advice just doesn’t cut it.

We need advice that is tailored to our specific sleep needs and problems. Personalised tools that give personalised predictions are essential.

Mathematical modelling

Sleep researchers have long used mathematical tools, or mathematical models, to understand sleep. For instance, the seminal two-process model of sleep regulation, developed in the early 1980s, shaped our understanding of sleep timing; our bed and rise times are regulated by the interaction of our body’s circadian “clock” and a homeostatic variable that accumulates sleep “pressure” as we continue to stay awake. Similarly, pioneering work by McCarley-Hobson in the 1970s used mathematical models to rationalise how distinct groups of neurons coordinate the transitions between the two main sleep stages: rapid eye movement (REM) and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.

The two-process and McCarley-Hobson models have both spawned numerous adaptations that have themselves been applied broadly, from predicting alertness in resident physicians to debating whether moving school start times will combat adolescent fatigue. The usefulness of these models comes from the fact that their variables can be related to measurable features of sleep. For example, the variables of the two-process model tell us about the onset and duration of sleep. In this way, models act as a mathematical playground in which we can simulate different sleep patterns and predict what sort of things might make sleep better or worse.

Of course, predictions are only helpful if they are tailored to that individual. And while available models are good at simulating the “average” person’s sleep, there are clinically important features of sleep that models haven’t yet fully considered. For example, preferred sleep timing varies a lot from person to person, with some people preferring to stay up late and others preferring to go to bed and wake up early.

Another feature of sleep is the cycling that occurs between NREM and REM sleep states across the night. In healthy young adults, NREM sleep predominates at the start of the night, and REM sleep predominates at the end of the night. This pattern is disrupted in sleep disorders and changes as we age.

In my PhD, I was curious as to whether existing models were able to simulate these two features of sleep. So I selected two models: one model – grounded in the two-process model – described sleep timing; the other model – built on the McCarley-Hobson model – described the cycling pattern between NREM and REM sleep. Next, I used theories from applied maths – coupled oscillator and geometric singular perturbation theories, to be precise – to uncover the geometric building blocks of each of the models. In doing so, I was able to discern what sort of sleep patterns could be constructed in model simulations.

When I looked at the first model, I saw that it had all the necessary mathematical building blocks to predict sleep timing in lots of different people. I could simulate sleep timing not just in the “average” person, but also in people with extreme “night owl” or “early bird” tendencies.

When it came to the second model, things were a bit more complicated. Its building blocks were put together in a way that meant that the model couldn’t simulate the predominance of NREM at the start of the night, and REM at the end of the night. However, I figured out a way to rearrange the model’s building blocks. The result? The model became more flexible, allowing me to simulate a progressive increase in REM duration across the night. All in all, my research showed that it is possible to make models that predict some of the key, finer details of sleep – the kind of details that vary from person to person.

Simulate your sleep

At the University of Surrey, we are developing digital tools, for both clinical and personal use, to help people calibrate models of their own sleep patterns. With a personalised model, it’s possible to simulate different lifestyle changes and predict which ones will be most effective at helping you get better sleep.

And the results might be surprisingly achievable – getting a good night’s sleep might be a matter of spending a short period out in the Sun each morning. You can see the impact light has on sleep with our online Visualisation Tools, available here.

Simulate your own sleep patterns.
University of Surrey

Disturbed sleep will still trouble many of us, but now with the help of mathematical models we can take a glimpse into a future where each one of us can say goodnight to those bad nights – and hello to better sleep in nights to come.

Rachel Bernasconi has received funding from the UKRI Higher Education Innovation Funding scheme, the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre and the University of Surrey.

articles.title: Should you correct a friend’s health myth? Ask yourself this question first
articles.summary:
Kaspars Grinvalds/Shutterstock.com

“You must drink eight glasses of water a day” is the kind of advice a friend might offer. But what the advice leaves out is that our daily fluid intake comes from a variety of sources, including other drinks and food.

Some health advice gets repeated so often that few people think to question where it came from. Some of these claims are harmless, even if they simplify what the science actually says.

So before correcting a family member or friend, ask yourself: could this belief change a decision about their medical care? If not, correcting it may achieve very little.

The water example is a good one. A review of the evidence has found limited support for the idea that everyone needs a fixed number of glasses each day. Our requirement varies with age, activity and environment. Even so, the simplified version may still encourage people to stay hydrated.

The same goes for other familiar beliefs: that wet hair causes colds, that chicken soup makes you better when you are ill, or that you should be aiming for 10,000 steps a day.

All are half-truths. The science is more complicated than the slogan, but the beliefs may still encourage healthy behaviour.

However, some claims are harder to overlook. What counts is whether the belief could affect a decision about medical care and increase the risk of illness.

Cancer specialists have warned about juice diets and coffee enemas being promoted as alternatives to treatments that have been shown to work. Unlike misconceptions about hydration or wet hair, these claims can influence whether someone accepts, delays or rejects medical care.

Someone who believes an alternative therapy can cure cancer may turn down treatment that could save their life.

Vaccination is another example. A parent who comes across misleading information online may decide to avoid or delay childhood vaccinations.

Across Europe and parts of central Asia, measles cases doubled in 2024 to their highest level since 1997. More than 40% of cases were in children under the age of five.

Measles is returning because of health misinformation.
Habanero Pixel / Shutterstock.com

The same applies when people choose supplements or alternative remedies instead of prescribed treatments. The trouble starts when someone believes that herbal remedies such as turmeric, or dietary changes, can replace treatments that have been shown to work.

People do not have to accept every recommendation a doctor makes, and they are entitled to decline treatment or seek a second opinion. Problems arise when decisions rest on misinformation about medical care. Informed choice depends on understanding the options, and misinformation distorts the information that choice is built on.

Facts alone won’t cut it

Even then, correcting someone is rarely straightforward. Being told you are wrong can feel judgmental, embarrassing and dismissive, particularly when a belief is tied to family traditions, personal experience or hope during a difficult time, such as a cancer diagnosis.

Research on misinformation consistently shows that people do not always abandon a belief when they are given the facts. Beliefs are often tied to identity, experience and values, rather than being a simple misunderstanding of the evidence.

As a nurse whose research examines how healthcare professionals respond to health misinformation, I have seen how rarely facts alone correct these claims.

How a conversation begins makes a difference. Telling a friend or relative outright that they are wrong may encourage resistance. An approach based on questioning is often more productive.

Asking where they heard the claim, what makes the source trustworthy, or whether they have discussed it with a healthcare professional can open a more constructive conversation. Pharmacists, doctors and other healthcare professionals remain an important source of clarification when there is uncertainty.

Health advice is often less tidy than the slogan. Sometimes the missing details make little difference, as with the water. Other times they change a decision about someone’s medical care.

Knowing which is which helps us decide which claims to let pass, and which are worth challenging.

Josh Sharman does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam’s tropical forests isn’t guaranteed
articles.summary:
Parilov/Shutterstock

Deep in the jungle of central Vietnam, the heat is heavy, the mosquitoes are relentless and the terrain offers no easy paths. My colleagues and I don’t hike on clear trails, we wade up riverbeds, stepping carefully over slippery rocks to access the thousands of trees we have been measuring for the last decade.

In 2024, I spent nearly two months camping in the forests of Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong, a nature reserve in central Vietnam. I worked with a field team of 12 people, in the gruelling conditions required to gather long-term ecological data.

Logging was particularly intense in the tropical forests of Vietnam between 1982 and 2007. As a result, the forest cover and the quality of those forest ecosystems has declined substantially. While forest cover in Vietnam has increased since the 1990s due to plantations and natural regeneration, the quality of forest recovery is less clear.

We visited every tree in our 24 study plots to measure them by hand in a meticulous, physically exhausting process that has been carried out four times since 2016. By identifying the species of each tree, measuring their diameter with a tape measure and noting any trees that have died, we tracked how these once-logged forests were recovering. Our findings challenge a key assumption about tropical forest regrowth.

Both governments and global carbon markets (a trading system that incentivises cuts in greenhouse gas emissions) invest in natural climate solutions. This often involves investing in schemes to plant new trees that absorb atmospheric carbon during photosynthesis in order to offset other carbon emissions. But these schemes rely heavily on an assumption: that once logging stops, tropical forests will naturally bounce back and recover, rapidly taking up carbon dioxide and storing it in growing trees.

In our latest study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, we show that rapid and predictable recovery may be overly optimistic.

Field researchers walk a measuring tape through dense trees to mark out a permanent forest plot in central Vietnam.
Amy Bennett, CC BY-ND

Since 2007, when selective logging in the region ended, these forests have not recovered as expected. Between 2016 and 2024, the forests showed no net increase in the carbon stored in their trunks and branches. The trees are still growing, but carbon gains from growth were almost entirely offset by tree deaths. Recovery rates were far below what the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates for the region and rates reported for comparable logged forests in Southeast Asia.

Heat restricts growth

Part of the explanation lies in the very conditions that made our fieldwork so challenging – rising temperatures. Since we have been monitoring these forests, temperatures have risen sharply, and we linked rising maximum temperatures to lower carbon gains. In 2024, the region where our forest plots are located endured severe, prolonged heatwaves in April and four in a row in August. Heat is already limiting tree growth here.

A field team member carries a ladder across a shallow, rocky river in Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong Nature Reserve, central Vietnam.
Amy Bennett, CC BY-NC-ND

These ecological constraints have financial and policy implications. Southeast Asia is central to carbon markets and the ecosystem restoration industry, hosting the majority of profitable forest restoration projects. Protecting young, regrowing forests from being cleared again helps limit greenhouse gas emissions by keeping the carbon already stored in the trees safe, as recovering forests are particularly vulnerable to repeated logging and clearing.

Yet, when calculating the value of protecting or restoring these forests, projects tend to assume steady, rapid tree growth, rather than measuring true forest function under the stress of extreme heat. Without long-term ground monitoring, schemes risk both underfunding necessary protection and overestimating carbon removal that may not be happening.

Despite harsh conditions and past disturbance, the forests managed to keep almost all the carbon stored in their trunks and branches intact. Long-term monitoring by our team and partners provided the evidence base that helped designate Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong as a nature reserve in 2020. Protection as a nature reserve has helped prevent further degradation through logging, securing these forests and the carbon they store.

Easy to overestimate

However, mechanisms allowing countries to work together toward their climate pledges under Article 6 of the Paris climate agreement tend to rely on generalised estimates of recovery. Those mechanisms also risk overestimating how much carbon recovering tropical forests can actually absorb.

To achieve realistic climate solutions in a warming world, policies must remain grounded in committed, local field surveys, no matter how hard those data are to collect.

Sleeping in hammocks in humid jungles, enduring insect swarms and battling steep terrain isn’t just about collecting data; this research offers a true insight into how forests are functioning in a changing world.

Amy Bennett has received funding from the Natural Environment Research Council, the European Research Council, the European Space Agency, the British Council, the Royal Society and the European Union.

articles.title: Lebanon facing uncertain future as UN peacekeepers prepare to depart
articles.summary:
Lebanon is facing an uncertain future, with the UN peacekeeping mission in the south of the country drawing to a close in December after nearly 50 years. The current situation is the most serious to confront Lebanon since my time serving there as a UN peacekeeper in 1982.

The withdrawal of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) is taking place against a backdrop of volatility. Conflict between the Israeli military and Hezbollah, a Lebanese armed group, has escalated in the past few years. This has caused repeated displacement, destruction of homes and infrastructure, civilian deaths and damage to agricultural land across the country.

From March 2026 to June, when a ceasefire in Lebanon was signed, at least 3,783 people were killed and 11,699 wounded in the conflict, according to the country’s health ministry. The death toll included 247 children, 363 women and 133 healthcare workers. At least 28 Israeli soldiers have been killed in Lebanon in the latest war, while four Israeli civilians have been killed in Hezbollah attacks.

Despite the ceasefire, Israeli forces continue military operations in southern Lebanon. These include airstrikes and shelling beyond the so-called security zone they reestablished earlier in 2026. Recent weeks have also seen extensive destruction of Lebanese civilian infrastructure and villages by the Israeli military.

The plan moving forward is for the Lebanese state to be the sole provider of security in the south of the country. But this is neither practical nor realistic. The Lebanese armed forces have neither the capacity or the capability to fulfil such a role.

New security framework

The decision to end Unifil’s mandate was made by the UN security council in August 2025. It followed intense political pressure from the US and Israel, who have argued the peacekeeping force has failed its mission by allowing Hezbollah to build military infrastructure near the Israeli border.

UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which provides the basis for the current Unifil operations, mandated that southern Lebanon should be free of armed personnel and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese armed forces and the over 7,000 UN peacekeepers.

A new security framework was agreed in June 2026 following talks between Lebanon, Israel and the US. Lebanon and Israel committed to a reciprocal and sequenced process whereby the Lebanese armed forces will restore effective sovereign authority over all Lebanese territory.

The Israel Defense Forces will then progressively redeploy out of Lebanese territory, pending the verified disarmament of non-state armed groups and dismantlement of their associated infrastructure.

However, this remains a distant prospect. Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected calls to disarm while Israel maintains a military presence in Lebanese territory.

Lebanon, along with some EU states, have sought agreement for a new peacekeeping force or presence from the US and other UN security council members. A range of options have been floated since the decision to end Unifil’s mandate, including a French proposal for a multinational European force that would operate alongside the Lebanese armed forces.

But none of these proposals have been acceptable to the US and Israel. The Israelis want any future role for an international force to include more than monitoring and reporting what is happening on the ground – the primary tasks performed by Unifil.

They insist such a force should be operationally integrated with Israel’s declared objectives of disarming Hezbollah and dismantling its infrastructure.

Nevertheless, the international community should not abandon Lebanon. One possible interim mechanism to fill the void left by Unifil’s withdrawal is to strengthen the presence in Lebanon of the UN Truce Supervision Organization (Untso) and its observer group.

Untso was the first peacekeeping mission to be established by the UN in 1948. Its military observers remain in the Middle East to monitor ceasefires, supervise armistice agreements and prevent isolated incidents from escalating. They also assist other UN peacekeeping operations in the region, including in Lebanon.

This interim measure would leave at least some UN presence on the ground in Lebanon to monitor the various parties to the conflict and report on what is happening there. Untso will remain in Lebanon after Unifil’s withdrawal. But pressure would need to be brought to bear on Israel and Hezbollah to facilitate a strengthened presence.

Consequences of Unifil withdrawal

The end of Unfil’s mandate poses a major security problem for Lebanon. Since 1978, Unifil has played a major stabilising and diplomatic role in Lebanon that is often not acknowledged. It has provided essential support to the Lebanese army and has historically facilitated negotiations between Israel and Lebanon.

Unifil’s withdrawal also threatens the loss of much-needed services in the south. UN peacekeepers have provided safe passage for humanitarian aid convoys and have helped restore damaged services such as healthcare and water.

The central issue now is what happens to civilian protection, independent monitoring and international oversight after Unifil leaves. Its exit comes at a time when access to southern Lebanon is already severely hampered by the scale of the destruction, unexploded ordnance and landmines.

Displaced Lebanese civilians must be allowed to return home and further destruction of civilian infrastructure must be prevented. But whether the new security framework can guarantee this is far from clear.

articles.title: England and Wales are in a winter drought – which could make next summer even drier
articles.summary:
Water levels in reservoirs in England are still low this winter. AndyGriffin/Shutterstock

Historically, Great Britain’s most severe water crises have been associated with dry winters.

The summer drought of 1976 was made worse by an exceptionally dry preceding winter. More recently, the dry winter of 2021/22 set the stage for the severe summer drought of 2022, especially in chalk aquifers of England.

A dry winter in early 2023, including the driest February in 30 years across England, prevented reservoirs in south-west England from refilling, extending hosepipe bans through an entire year and stressing river ecosystems.

The drought of 2026 in parts of England and Wales is still evolving, but recent data shows that the very dry summer conditions from June to August have continued. There was below average rainfall, and lingering low river and groundwater levels, into early October. Catchment areas where there are dry conditions in the winter have the potential to have more severe summer drought conditions next year. However, rainfall in November has started to hit normal levels for the time of year.

Why dry winters are important

Drought is normally thought of as a summertime phenomenon. Extremely hot weather drives up water demand for crops and public supply, as seen during the widespread hosepipe bans and irrigation water restrictions across England and Wales in the summer of 2026. However, droughts also occur during the cooler winter months when rainfall drops below normal.

What happened during the drought of 1976.

Because British winters are typically wetter than summers, a winter drought rarely feels like a problem, especially as most of us prefer crisp, dry winter days to cold, wet weather.

Yet winter is the critical window when low evaporation and dormant vegetation allow rain to infiltrate through the soil and replenish underground aquifers and reservoirs.

When winter droughts occur, the impact often emerges months later in spring and summer as that deficit moves slowly through the hydrological system. This delay is particularly pronounced in regions reliant on groundwater for public supply and river flow, such as the chalk catchments of east and south-east England and the sandstones of the Midlands. Because water takes months or even years to percolate through soil and porous rock, a winter rainfall shortage can impact river flows and groundwater levels the following summer.

Groundwater levels in England and Wales, summer (left) and October 2026 (right)

The maps show the rank (1 = driest) of the summer (Jun-Aug) and October 2026 groundwater levels.
Graph using data from Jonghun Kam and Seunghui Choi, Pohang University of Science and Technology., CC BY-NC-SA

Low winter rainfall strongly dictates summer groundwater levels as well as river flow levels, substantially increasing the odds of a summer drought.

Seasonal rainfall forecasts for the rest of this winter indicate there will be a recovery from the summer’s drought conditions for much of England and Wales, but a heightened chance for drought to persist in the south, east and northeast. This means that some parts of England could already be banking a hidden water deficit for next summer.

Whether winter droughts are becoming more frequent or severe with climate change remains unclear from the historical record alone. However, future climate projections point to a critical shift in how the seasons interact. By 2070, UK winters are projected to become up to 20% wetter, and summers significantly drier.

Wetter winters will not eliminate winter droughts. Year-to-year atmospheric variability means dry winters will still occur, and hotter, drier summers are likely to leave soils much drier by autumn. Much early winter rain will be absorbed simply re-wetting dry soils and meeting higher demand, shortening the seasonal window to top up groundwater levels and altering the link between winter rain and summer water supplies.

How to deal with winter droughts

Summer droughts in England and Wales are becoming increasingly disruptive, not only through agricultural irrigation restrictions and domestic hosepipe bans like those in 2026, but also by hampering river navigation, damaging freshwater ecosystems, and even curtailing electricity generation from power stations reliant on river cooling water, which can drive up energy prices.

As water demand rises alongside a growing population and a push for national food security, water planners need to track how winter rains top up the water system as well as summer demand.

Society must also shift from responding to summer water shortages to enhancing year-round water storage.

This includes building more reservoirs on farms to help supply agricultural crops, actively pumping excess winter floodwater into underground aquifers (an underground layer that retains water), and restoring wetlands to slow runoff from the land.

These measures could help mitigate the increasing pressure on our water systems as climate change creates warmer and drier weather more frequently.

Justin Sheffield receives funding from UKRI and European Space Agency.

articles.title: We’ve documented almost 1,000 years lost to wrongful convictions across Europe – and we’re still counting
articles.summary:
NewAfrica/Shutterstock

It was a cold October night in 2001 when Rudolf Rupp, a 52-year-old farmer from a small town in Bavaria, Germany, vanished. He had gone out drinking at a local bar, as he often did, and never came home. His wife reported him missing, but no one could find a trace of him or his car. For almost two years, it was as if he had just vanished into thin air. No clues, no body. Just silence.

Then the rumours started.

Neighbours gossiped that something terrible had happened at the farm – and that Rupp’s family had killed him. The police began to suspect his wife, two teenage daughters, and the boyfriend of one of the girls. All four eventually confessed.

The story they told was gruesome: that Rudolf had been ambushed, beaten to death, cut into pieces, and disposed of by feeding him to the farm dogs. The case, especially the grisly details of the confessions, drew nationwide media attention in Germany.

But soon after, they took it all back, saying they had been pressured by investigators and that their confessions were not true. They all had intellectual disabilities, and they said they were coerced by police.

In 2005, despite the fact that no body or any type of evidence was found, they were convicted based solely on those confessions. Even though they had recanted their confessions and insisted they were innocent.

The Insights section is committed to high-quality longform journalism. Our editors work with academics from many different backgrounds who are tackling a wide range of societal and scientific challenges.

Then, in 2009, eight years after Rupp vanished, his car was pulled from a river. His remains were inside, still in one piece, sitting in the driver’s seat. There were no signs that he had been beaten up or cut up. The horrifying story the family had told could not possibly have happened.

The case was reopened, and in a full retrial before the Landshut Regional Court the family was acquitted in 2011. They spent several years in prison for a crime they did not commit, a story they had confessed to under pressure.

No one ever formally investigated how the family’s specific confessions were extracted. The family’s defence had long claimed coercion, and over time some corroborating evidence emerged.

Police had filmed themselves having the suspects “reconstruct” the crime at the farm, and a criminal law professor who later reviewed that footage described the officers’ approach as inquisitorial and leading, saying suspects simply could not be questioned that way.

Separately, a scrap dealer whom police suspected of disposing of Rupp’s car testified at the retrial that, when he would not give the statement investigators wanted, an officer from the same police unit held a service weapon to his head. No officer was investigated. Instead, prosecutors put the scrap dealer on trial for making a false accusation. In December 2012, the court acquitted him.

All four family members were described by their defence lawyer as having cognitive vulnerabilities, which made them especially susceptible to coercive questioning. And although it became clear the family had confessed to something they did not do, they were never compensated, because the retrial court held them partly responsible for their own false statements.

Sadly, the Rupp case is far from unique.

Wrongful convictions and the EUREX database

When Ina Post addressed the audience at the European Innocence Network meeting in Amsterdam in 2019, the room fell silent. Her presence was calm, but the weight of her story was overwhelming.

In 1986, she was wrongfully convicted in the Netherlands of murdering an elderly woman she cared for. The only evidence was a confession. A confession she gave after hours of intense, suggestive police interrogation while in a psychologically vulnerable state. There was no forensic proof, and much of what she had said turned out to be factually incorrect. Still, it took more than two decades of legal struggle before she was finally acquitted in 2010.

Listening to her that day was deeply moving. The room was silent – you could have heard a pin drop. Her story was not just about what had happened to her, it was about how easily justice can go wrong, and how hard it is to make it right again. Her words stayed with us.

As researchers in the field of false confessions and wrongful convictions, we asked ourselves: how many others have suffered similar fates? We knew that the United States tracked exoneration cases through the National Registry of Exonerations, but Europe had no central database, no coordinated effort to track wrongful convictions. There were no numbers, no overview of the problem and no one was trying to change that.

That is why we created EUREX – the European Registry of Exonerations. Its mission is to archive and analyse exonerations across Europe. EUREX is a centralised database that collects and publishes information about cases where individuals were wrongfully convicted and later cleared of all charges.

Beyond documenting these cases, EUREX seeks to understand their causes and consequences, identify systemic patterns, and ultimately contribute to improving legal decision-making. In the long run, we aim to lead empirical research that tests these patterns and informs reforms to prevent future miscarriages of justice.

Wrongful convictions are often thought of as rare and tragic mistakes. But the reality is more complex.

So far, we have documented 150 cases in 20 countries since 1981 in which people were officially declared innocent after years – sometimes decades – behind bars.

Together, these individuals lost more than 970 years of freedom. Our first systematic analysis of the registry (covering the first 144 cases and published in 2026 in Forensic Science International: Synergy) showed that most had been convicted of very serious crimes such as murder or sexual assault. This highlights the devastating consequences when errors occur in high-stakes trials.

Read more:
‘People think you come out … and live happily ever after. If only.’ The reality of life after wrongful conviction

These numbers are exactly why a project like EUREX matters: at its launch, Saul Kassin, a social psychologist who specialises in false confessions, described the registry as filling a real gap in the field, one that could give researchers, legal practitioners, and policymakers across Europe a shared evidence base for understanding how wrongful convictions happen – something that has been missing until now.

Innocence lawyer, Geert-Jan Knoops, speaking at the same event, put it more bluntly: “With EUREX, we now have objective proof that we are not dealing with isolated incidents.”

False confessions

Across the world, false confessions have played a significant role in wrongful convictions. For example, about 35% of the cases in EUREX involve someone who confessed to a crime they did not commit.

Research shows that often false confessions happen to the most vulnerable: teenagers, people with intellectual disabilities, and those with mental health issues. Under pressure in a police interrogation, they may say what the interrogators want to hear – just to get out of the room. In many cases, the combination of personal vulnerabilities and stressful surroundings creates a powerful mix of factors that can lead to a false confession.

Scientists have identified three types of false confessions: voluntary, coerced-compliant and coerced-internalised. A voluntary false confession happens when someone steps forward without any pressure, often to protect someone else, gain attention, or because they mistakenly believe confessing will benefit them. Coerced-compliant confessions occur when a suspect knows they are innocent but gives in simply to end the interrogation or secure what seems like a better deal. Finally, coerced-internalised confessions are the most disturbing: after intense questioning, a person may start doubting their own memory and come to believe they committed the crime.

The kind that shows up most often in courts is the coerced one. These confessions typically follow hours of questioning, psychological manipulation, and physical or emotional exhaustion. Suspects may be deprived of sleep, denied breaks, or led to believe that confessing is the only way out. Without a lawyer present, vulnerable people are especially likely to agree to whatever investigators suggest.

False confession expert Gisli Gudjonsson, writing in a Frontiers in Psychology editorial summarising his own 40-year review of the science, explained: “Until detailed analysis of real-life cases, peer-reviewed research, and DNA exonerations began to emerge in the 1980s and 1990s, it was widely believed that only those with intellectual disabilities or mental illness were susceptible to giving false confessions. This ‘common sense’ view is a fallacy. False confessions are caused by a dynamic process and a combination of ‘risk factors’, which is not confined to the mentally impaired. In fact, most of those who give a coerced confession to police are not mentally impaired.”

Once a confession is made, even if it is false and there is no other evidence, it can shape how everyone sees the case, from law enforcement to judges. It becomes hard to undo. Generally, people assume that no one would confess to something they did not do, so distinguishing false confessions from genuine ones is extremely challenging.

That is why the story of the Rupp family should serve as a warning about what can go wrong when confessions are treated as proof, even when there is no other evidence.

How widespread is the problem?

And yet, these numbers only tell part of the story. EUREX uses a deliberately strict definition: it only includes cases in which someone was convicted by final judgment and later officially cleared after the case was reopened, through an acquittal or a formal declaration of innocence. Countless other cases never clear that bar. Doubts may linger for years, new evidence may surface too late, or legal hurdles, procedural limits and institutional resistance may close the door before a case can be reopened at all. The real number of wrongful convictions is almost certainly higher than any registry can capture.

It is hard to say whether wrongful convictions themselves are becoming more or less frequent. What does seem to be rising is our ability and willingness to catch them. More than half of the exonerations we found happened after 2010, which probably reflects growing efforts to revisit old cases, improve fair investigative practices, and develop more transparent review processes.

One thing the registry makes clear is that wrongful convictions can happen to almost anyone. Exonerees come from different countries, income levels, professions, and ethnic backgrounds. Most are men, but this mirrors the prison population as a whole: men account for the vast majority of people convicted of serious crimes such as murder and sexual assault.

As Saul Kassin, who has spent decades studying wrongful convictions, said in an interview with us:

These are not all the same types of people. This is not about who they are. There are men and women, adults and children, people speaking different languages, from different countries and with different skin colours. Exonerations aren’t limited to a certain type of person – it is a systemic problem.

Hundreds of years wasted behind bars.
shutterstock/ninoon

Wrongful convictions aren’t explained by who the exonerated individuals are, but by what they lose. On average, the exonerees we found were about 36 years old at the time of their conviction – an age when most people are building careers, starting families, and laying plans for the future. Losing those years leaves scars that are personal, social, and financial all at once.

In subsequent interviews, Ina Post has described what that loss feels like: “I was 30 years old when I was arrested. I was married. My husband and I wanted children. While I was in detention, I decided to get a divorce. When you are imprisoned, you rob your partner of their life, too.”

Wrongful convictions are better understood not as a matter of who is convicted, but of how convictions come about. The patterns identified by these cases reflect precisely this: recurring flaws in the processes that produce them.

False confessions, like the ones at the centre of the Rupp and Post cases, appear in 35% of cases we have examined. Flawed forensic evidence played a role in 24%, a reminder that scientific-sounding evidence is only as reliable as the people collecting, evaluating and interpreting it. Eyewitness misidentification (23%) and false accusations (35%) round out the list, underlining just how fallible human memory and perception can be under pressure.

One of the registry’s most striking findings concerns what happens to the actual perpetrator. In 91 cases, an innocent person was convicted for a crime committed by someone else, and in roughly 40% of those, the real culprit was never identified at all.

That means the system failed twice: once by punishing the wrong person, and again by leaving the guilty one free. As Kassin warns: “When you close a case on an innocent person, you leave the offender free to reoffend – and they often do.”

The scale of this risk is stark: a study of 109 real perpetrators later identified in the United States found that 94% went on to commit further crimes, including murder, while innocent people sat behind bars in their place. Failing to catch the true offender does not just deny justice to the wrongfully convicted; it puts the public in danger.

‘My nightmare is over’ – Tomasz Komenda

On New Year’s Eve 1996, 15-year-old Małgorzata Kwiatkowska vanished after a party in Miłoszyce, a small village in south-western Poland. What started as a festive New Year’s Eve ended tragically when her dead body was discovered in the snow the next morning. She had been raped and left to die of internal injuries and hypothermia. The crime scene revealed multiple DNA profiles, bite marks, and other forensic clues – yet for years, the case went cold.

Then, in 2000, a TV programme about the unsolved murder aired a composite sketch of a man seen with Małgorzata on the night she disappeared. A viewer tipped off police, claiming it resembled Tomasz Komenda. Despite thin physical evidence and an alibi that held up, Komenda was arrested, charged, and while insisting he was innocent, convicted in 2003. He was sentenced to 15 years, later extended to 25 years on appeal.

Because Komenda refused to admit guilt, he was ineligible for parole. Over nearly two decades in prison, he endured physical abuse, isolation, and psychological torment, and attempted suicide more than once. “I thought I would never get out,” he later told TVN24. “I thought they would kill me in prison”.

The case cracked open in 2016, when a police officer reviewing old cases spotted major flaws in the original investigation. New DNA testing excluded Komenda entirely and instead pointed to two other men.

Komenda walked free on March 15, 2018, after 18 years in prison. That May, the Polish Supreme Court formally overturned his conviction and declared him innocent. Standing on the courtroom steps after spending 6,540 days behind bars for a crime he did not commit, Komenda told reporters: “My nightmare is over”.

But freedom did not erase what prison had done to him. In a television interview Komenda described how fear and anxiety followed him into daily life. “Even now, I get scared when I hear a loud noise. I still dream about the prison”.

In 2021, he was awarded nearly 13 million zloty (about €2.75 million) in compensation for the years he had lost. But, as he and many other exonerees have said, no amount of money can make up for the lost years.

Psychological research supports what Komenda described. A landmark 2004 study found that wrongfully convicted people often develop post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and other lasting emotional wounds. In some cases it is severe enough to resemble the aftermath of torture.

A later systematic review reached a similar conclusion, observing that the psychological toll of being wrongfully accused is often severe and long-lasting, and that it can quietly erode someone’s sense of identity, health, relationships, finances, and trust in institutions, while adding a lingering social stigma.

That stigma tends to outlast the conviction itself. Even after exoneration, many people struggle to find work, secure housing, and rebuild a social life. They are often without any of the structured support that is typically offered to parolees. So in practice, being cleared of a crime does not always mean the sentence is over. For many exonerees, it just becomes a different kind of life sentence.

For Komenda, that second sentence was cruelly brief. In May 2024, he died of cancer at just 46 years old. His case prompted a national reckoning in Poland over police misconduct and flawed forensic work, and it pushed the question of how Europe treats exonerees onto the wider public agenda.

Wrongful convictions are not just legal failures. They are human ones. Komenda’s story is a painful reminder of the damage they do and of how long the road to healing can be, even after freedom is won.

Addressing the problem

Across Europe, reform has often come in the wake of scandal. In the Netherlands, the Schiedammer Park murder case exposed serious flaws in investigative practices and prosecutorial oversight. Public outrage led the College of Procurators General to set up the Commissie-Posthumus in 2005.

Its landmark report identified real vulnerabilities in how criminal cases were built and recommended concrete fixes; among them, bringing in independent forensic advisors and building explicit safeguards against “tunnel vision” – the tendency for investigators to fixate on one suspect and stop questioning their own theory.

These recommendations also led to the creation of the Adviescommissie Afgesloten Strafzaken (ACAS) in 2012, an advisory body that can recommend cases for reopening when new evidence casts doubt on a conviction.

Norway has gone further still, establishing a Criminal Cases Review Commission with full statutory powers to reopen convictions whenever significant new evidence emerges (unlike the Dutch ACAS, which can only advise the Prosecutor General and does not have the power to reopen cases itself).

By December 2020, the Norwegian commission had reopened 351 cases. One of its most striking successes is the case of Viggo Kristiansen, convicted in 2001 (and again on appeal in 2002) of raping and murdering two young girls in Kristiansand, and given Norway’s maximum sentence at the time: 21 years. The case against him rested on a co-defendant’s testimony, weak DNA traces, and a psychological profile. Kristiansen spent nearly two decades insisting he was innocent and filing appeals that went nowhere.

Then in 2021, the commission agreed to reopen the case: new DNA testing excluded him, and witness statements that had previously been dismissed turned out to support his alibi after all. In December 2022, the Borgarting Court of Appeal acquitted him outright, concluding his co-defendant had acted alone. Kristiansen later received substantial compensation. His case makes the argument for independent review bodies: they give a wrongful conviction a real, structured path back to court.

In the United Kingdom, concerns about miscarriages of justice led to the creation of a dedicated review body in 1997 – the Criminal Cases Review Commission. But the watchdog has been plunged into crisis and faced relentless criticism about the way it has handled recent cases.

Read more:
The miscarriage of justice watchdog is failing at its only job – here’s how to fix it

But such safeguards are far from universal. For example, Belgium and Portugal record zero exonerations in the registry, almost certainly not because their justice systems get it right every time, but because structural barriers make miscarriages of justice harder to surface or overturn in the first place. Narrow rules for reopening closed cases, no independent review commission, and limited legal aid after conviction all add up to a system where mistakes can simply stay buried.

At the European level, the gap is even wider. Criminal justice is still handled almost entirely at the national level, and there’s no EU-wide framework for catching or correcting wrongful convictions. Human rights law offers broad principles, but not the practical tools needed to identify and fix specific errors.

“One does not easily get past 24 lost years,” said Post, who spent four years in prison and more than two decades fighting to finally clear her name.

Wrongful convictions will never be eliminated entirely, but they can be made rarer, easier to detect, and faster to repair. Independent review commissions, safeguards against coercive interrogations, and robust forensic standards are not abstract ideals – they are practical steps grounded in evidence.

Building these reforms into national systems and pooling what is learned across borders is how Europe makes sure that justice does not fail the very people it is meant to protect.

articles.title: How to recognise when video gaming becomes an addiction
articles.summary:
Gaming disorder can develop when someone loses control over their gaming habits and continues to play despite negative effects on their everyday life. Studio Nut/Shutterstock

Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) formally recognised gaming disorder in its International Classification of Diseases. It describes a persistent pattern in which someone loses control over gaming, gives it priority over other activities and continues playing despite harmful consequences. For a diagnosis, the behaviour must seriously affect everyday life, usually for at least 12 months.

The diagnosis has prompted debate. Gaming brings enjoyment and social connection to millions of people, and researchers disagree about where intense involvement ends and a clinical problem begins.

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association included “internet gaming disorder” in its diagnostic manual. However, it classified it as a condition requiring further study rather than an established diagnosis. The WHO subsequently adopted its own diagnostic criteria for gaming disorder.

I have researched problematic gaming for decades, beginning with work examining similarities between video games and slot machines. Researchers use terms such as “excessive gaming”, “problematic gaming” and “gaming addiction”, sometimes interchangeably. I regard addiction as the extreme end of a spectrum of gaming-related difficulties. The crucial question is whether someone is losing control and experiencing harm.

Why some people are more vulnerable

In a review of research, my colleagues and I examined what may contribute to the development of gaming disorder. We found that no single factor explains it. Personality, motivations for playing, mental health, biological differences and the design of games can all play a part.

Research has repeatedly found an association between gaming disorder and a personality trait known as neuroticism. People with higher levels of neuroticism tend to be more sensitive to stress and more prone to negative emotions.

People who experience more anxiety or distress may find virtual worlds reassuring or easier to control than their everyday circumstances. Gaming can offer temporary relief, but relying on it to escape difficulties may become problematic.

Gaming disorder has been linked to depression and anxiety. Research also suggests that people with ADHD or autism may be more likely to develop problems with gaming. Some studies have found a link between problematic gaming and suicidal thoughts, although this does not mean that gaming causes them.

However, much of this research on mental health examines people’s gaming habits and mental health at a single point in time. We cannot assume that gaming causes these difficulties, or that they necessarily cause gaming disorder. The relationship may work in both directions.

Studies using brain scans have identified differences in the brains of some people with problematic gaming. These differences occur in areas involved in how people respond to rewards, make decisions and control their behaviour.

Similar findings have been reported in research on other addictions. However, we cannot tell from these studies whether the brain differences existed before the gaming problems began or developed alongside them.

The games people choose may also matter. “Massively multiplayer online role-playing games” have frequently been associated with problematic gaming. In these games, large numbers of players share a virtual world that continues to exist even when they log off.

Researchers have also identified links with shooting and strategy games. But games vary considerably, as do the people who play them. A game’s genre alone does not make it addictive.

Game design can encourage repeated play through challenges, achievements and rewards. Some rewards arrive unpredictably, giving players a reason to try again because the next attempt might bring something valuable.

Psychologists call one form of this “variable-ratio reinforcement”. Players receive rewards but cannot predict how many attempts it will take to earn them. Such reward systems can help explain why some players find it difficult to stop, although their effects differ from person to person.

There are also concerns about how some games make money. Some games offer microtransactions, which allow players to spend real money on items or features within the game. These include loot boxes, which provide random virtual rewards without players knowing exactly what they will receive. The resemblance to gambling has attracted particular attention because loot boxes can be available to children.

A systematic review of research found associations between spending on loot boxes and both problematic gambling and gaming. However, this evidence does not establish that buying loot boxes causes either condition. Nor does it establish that buying loot boxes leads people into gambling later.

When should someone seek help?

One warning sign is being unable to cut back on gaming despite repeated attempts. Others include withdrawing from relationships or losing interest in other activities. Some people continue playing even when gaming is seriously affecting their work or education.

Some people become irritable or anxious when they cannot play, or conceal how much time they spend gaming. No single warning sign is enough to diagnose gaming disorder, but ongoing problems deserve attention.

If gaming is taking over someone’s life, they can seek help from a GP or mental health professional. These professionals can help assess the problem and determine whether specialist support is needed.

In England, the NHS also has a National Centre for Gaming Disorders, which provides specialist support for people aged 13 and over.

It is equally important to remember that many people play for long periods without suffering any harm. As I have argued throughout my research, the difference between a healthy enthusiasm and an addiction is that one adds to life while the other takes away from it.

Dr. Mark Griffiths has received research funding from a wide range of organizations including the Economic and Social Research Council, the British Academy, the Responsibility in Gambling Trust, and Norsk Tipping. He has also carried out consultancy for numerous gaming companies in the area of social responsibility and responsible gaming (including Camelot Plc). Views expressed here are his own and not those of these funding bodies.

articles.title: Controversial Netflix hit The Body blends 2000s nostalgia, Catholic satire and queer longing
articles.summary:
As far as TV episode titles go, you would be hard-pressed to find many more inflammatory than “Slutty God”. Opening Netflix’s new hit show The Body, the provocation neatly sets the tone for the unholy antics of the rebellious Catholic schoolgirls at the centre of the drama. At the same time, it encapsulates the divisive response that has embroiled the series.

The Body has been both praised by many queer viewers for its portrayal of lesbian desire, and condemned by over 100,000 petitioners for what they dub “blasphemous” content. But for fans of queer cinema, The Body’s artfully crafted opposition between Catholicism and sapphism, God and the gays, is nothing new. The film industry has long used this seeming incompatibility as a point of tension.

In featuring implausible visions, hyperbolic satanic panic and improvised rituals within a Catholic high school, The Body combines the established cinematic themes of isolated community and satirical blasphemy. One group exorcism devolves into hilarity as schoolgirls each confess their deepest sins – “I’m not a natural blonde!”, “I’m part of the fucking chess club!”, “I masturbate to Daddy Franklin [the school’s resident priest]!” The scene removes all the power from the moralistic structures that demand their piety.

The trailer for The Body.

Set in the 2000s, The Body pairs a nostalgic soundtrack with a heavily rhinestoned wardrobe. It features a lesbian storyline between Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), the popular co-captains of the Catholic high school’s all-girl dance team.

Rather than disparaging Christianity, The Body’s ethereal dance numbers and hypnotic party montages reimagine queer girlhood as an alternative to institutional religion.

These scenes capture what film studies researcher Catherine Wheatley identifies as an emerging tradition of “postsecular” cinema. That is, works that play with the boundaries between belief and unbelief, questioning both the certainty of the theist and the atheist. That approach offers “enchantment, awe and wonder without the politicising constraints of traditional religious faith”.

In what is quickly becoming one of the show’s most beloved scenes, Anya and Elise perform an emotional dance duet to Jeff Buckley’s Lover, You Should’ve Come Over. The camera revolves around the two actors as the surrounding spotlights are successively switched off. The dark background increasingly contrasts against their all-white costumes and plunges the couple into an otherworldly bubble.

The cast of The Body watch Anya and Elise’s duet scene.

It’s a transcendent experience in which the girls move in unison in a way that enables them to lose track of their social inhibitions. The awe on display here is not for God, but for the gut-wrenching, all-consuming power of a queer teenage crush.

Catholicism and queerness at the cinema

On-screen portrayals of Christianity and queerness have seen a notable surge in the past decade. Many films showcase the inner turmoil of a closeted protagonist, often within an insulated religious group, as in You Can Live Forever (2022).

Others intensify that conflict by focusing on so-called “conversion therapies”. Examples include Boy Erased (2018), Fair Haven (2016) and The Miseducation of Cameron Post (2018). The latter stars The Body’s creator Quinn Shephard as Cameron’s girlfriend.

But I’m A Cheerleader (1999) is perhaps the most iconic lesbian conversion drama. It bridges two popular approaches in queer Christian films: stories about conversion therapy and comedies that mock religious homophobia rather than leaning into heavy drama.

Falling loosely within this category, the nunsploitation trend of the 1970s has found a renaissance in The Little Hours (2017) and Benedetta (2021). Both films feature lesbian themes in their irreverent critiques of Christianity and power.

This boom in queer religious media seems to be symptomatic of the progressively increasing influence of Christian nationalism on politics, particularly in the US. Some of the 21st century’s most heated debates have revolved around the role of religion in shaping legislation. Key examples include the overturning of Roe v Wade in 2022 and the rollout of various anti-trans measures since Donald Trump’s re-election.

As partisanship deepens and the far right gains ground, growing numbers of Republicans are embracing ideas aligned with Christian nationalism. Meanwhile, Democrats face pressure to shift further to the right, a dynamic that both fuels and appeases rising anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment across the US.

The petition calling for The Body to be cancelled claims that “Netflix would never do this to Muslim or Hindu families”. That argument only reinforces the link between the backlash against the series and an idealised vision of a white, heteronormative Christian nation. A nation often framed by Trump’s rhetoric as being under threat.

Through its creative choices, Shephard’s series directly challenges the assumption of Christian dominance that anchors this worldview. Displacing the centrality of Catholic belief systems through a humorous irreverence and a transcendent queer desire, The Body manages to offer political critique while packaging it all in a highly marketable aesthetic.

Ultimately, the show turns what critics call blasphemy into something joyful, stylish and hard to ignore. It’s a reminder to viewers that queer desire needs no permission from tradition to feel sacred.

Ellie Smith receives funding from the Arts and Humanities Research Council to support the research undertaken as part of her PhD

articles.title: Gene therapy for blindness moves closer to patients
articles.summary:
EduBFoto/Shutterstock.com

Some people who had lost almost all their sight to an inherited eye disease could find objects on a table again after a single gene injection and training with special goggles.

None could read or recognise a face, but before treatment, the best any of them could see was a hand moving in front of the eye.

The results come from a small trial recently published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

A related gene treatment that needs no goggles is under review by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is due to decide by mid-2027 whether to approve it for patients. It would be the first treatment of its kind to win approval.

Both rely on optogenetics, the technique recognised with this year’s Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. In retinitis pigmentosa, the inherited disease in these trials, the eye’s light-catching cells slowly die. The nerve cells wired to them often survive, but cannot sense light.

Read more:
How pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain

Optogenetics uses a harmless virus to give the surviving cells a gene for a light-sensitive protein. It is like fixing a camera with a broken sensor by making its wiring sense light.

In the goggle trial, ten blind adults received the gene in one eye and then wore goggles that turn the scene into pulses of amber light. Seven became more sensitive to light. Four of these seven also did consistently better at tasks such as finding objects on a table when wearing the goggles.

The first patient, described in 2021, could touch a notebook almost every time while wearing the goggles, but a box of staples only a third of the time. The patient also reported being able to spot the white stripes of a pedestrian crossing.

The therapy under FDA review, called Mogenry, needs no goggles because its protein responds to everyday light. Its main trial enrolled 27 adults who could not make out from 20 feet (6.1 meters) what most people see from 1,600 feet.

A year later, treated patients could, on average, read about three more lines on a low-vision chart, while those given a dummy injection barely changed. That is a real gain, though far from reading a newspaper or driving.

How the same scene might look with advanced age-related macular degeneration.
Merve Sen, CC BY

What about a far more common form of sight loss?

Retinitis pigmentosa is rare. Age-related macular degeneration is not. An estimated 196 million people had it in 2020, and that number is projected to rise to 288 million by 2040.

Age-related macular degeneration damages the macula, the small central patch of the retina we use to read and recognise faces. The light-sensing cells there depend on supporting cells beneath them. In our lab in Tübingen, we study how a common genetic risk factor affects these cells and the thin layer they sit on.

With age, that layer thickens and fills with deposits. The supporting cells become stressed and dysfunctional, and the light-sensing cells that depend on them die.

In one late form, called geographic atrophy, it leaves a blank patch in the middle of whatever a person looks at. The patch slowly grows and central vision is lost. As a result, people can no longer read, recognise faces or watch TV, although their side vision remains.

Two drugs approved in the US slow its spread but cannot bring back lost sight. Optogenetics might, because nerve cells inside these patches often survive. The company behind Mogenry plans a trial in geographic atrophy, but it has not started yet.

The evidence is still thin. The goggle trial had ten people and no comparison group, and Mogenry’s main trial treated just 18 people. After four years, only about four in ten Mogenry patients could still read three extra lines. For a treatment given only once, we do not yet know how long the benefit lasts.

Read more:
Nobel laureate Karl Deisseroth on how light is changing what we know about the brain

Both treatments are a single injection into the eye rather than an operation, but the goggles are bulky and take training to use well. Side-effects were mostly mild or moderate inflammation and raised eye pressure.

Suitable patients are likely to be adults who have already lost almost all their sight but whose eyes can still send signals to the brain, with no other serious eye damage.

Cost will also decide who gets it.

Luxturna, an earlier gene therapy that replaces one faulty gene through eye surgery, launched in the US at US$425,000 per eye (£326,040).

An independent US institute judged that Mogenry would be fair value at US$67,400 to US$101,300 per eye.

The institute’s experts said most eye doctors would be able to administer Mogenry in their clinics. Approval is expected first in the US and Japan, which has granted priority review. No application for approval in Europe has yet been announced.

Optogenetics is unlikely to restore normal sight any time soon. In the next few years, key developments to watch include the FDA’s decision on Mogenry and its price, longer-term results from larger groups of patients (the current follow-up extends to four years) and findings from the first trial of optogenetics in people with geographic atrophy.

For now, optogenetics returns a sliver of sight to a small group of people, and the coming years will show whether that sliver becomes brighter.

Marius Ueffing receives funding from
Helmut Ecker Foundation, EU, BMFTR, German Research Council, DFG

Merve Sen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Climate change could dramatically alter habitats for Britain’s birds of prey – new research
articles.summary:
Few wildlife spectacles in the UK are quite as impressive as watching a peregrine
falcon dive towards its prey or a white-tailed eagle soar above the Scottish coastline.

Many of our birds of prey have made remarkable recoveries in recent decades,
following historical declines caused by shooting or poisoning, as well as exposure to environmental pollutants.

The red kite, once confined to a small part of Wales, is now a familiar sight across much of Britain. But as our climate changes, these birds face a new
conservation challenge.

My new research, published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, suggests that climate change could substantially alter which parts of the UK provide suitable environmental conditions for breeding birds of prey. However, what could be good news for some species may be considerably less encouraging for others.

Like all wildlife, birds of prey have particular environmental requirements.
Temperature and rainfall can influence where they live, when they breed and the
availability of the animals they feed on.

To investigate how our birds of prey might respond to future climate change, I used
computer models to estimate changes in environmental suitability for 16 species that breed in the UK, including eagles, falcons, hawks and owls.

By combining records of where these birds are currently found with information about their environment, I explored how suitable conditions might change over the coming decades. I considered several different projections of our future climate to account for some of the uncertainty surrounding these changes.

What struck me most was just how differently individual species could respond to the same changes in climate. The peregrine falcon is the world’s fastest animal, reaching speeds of more than 186 mph (300km/h) while diving for prey.

The falcon could see a considerable expansion in environmentally suitable areas across the UK. Under a high emissions scenario, my models projected an average increase of around 74% by the 2070s.

For other species, however, the picture looks rather different. My research suggests that the white-tailed eagle, short-eared owl, red kite and merlin could all experience reductions in suitable habitat. Under the same emissions scenario, the short-eared owl could experience a reduction of suitable area of around two-thirds.

The reliability of my models also varied between species, meaning that some
projections, including those for the peregrine falcon, should be interpreted with
caution.

These contrasting projections highlight an important challenge for wildlife conservation. Even species that occupy similar ecological roles and live in the same country may face very different futures.

A changing landscape

Of course, identifying new areas of environmental suitability does not necessarily
mean that birds of prey will move into them. A peregrine falcon will still need access to suitable nesting sites and sufficient prey to establish a breeding territory.

Under one emissions scenario, the short-eared owl could experience a reduction of suitable area of around two-thirds.
Paul Sawer

Equally, a projected reduction in the suitable conditions does not necessarily mean that a species will disappear from an area. Animals may be able to adapt to
changing conditions in ways that computer models cannot fully capture.

Climate change may also affect birds of prey indirectly. Changes in the abundance
and distribution of their prey, from small mammals to other birds, could have
important consequences for these predators.

Understanding these complex ecological relationships will be an important next step
in predicting how birds of prey might respond to a changing world.
Conserving our future birds of prey

Much of our approach to wildlife conservation involves protecting species in the
places where they are currently found. But what happens when the environmental
conditions that make these places suitable begin to change?

Public monitoring

Identifying areas that could remain suitable for birds of prey, as well as those that might become suitable in the future, could help inform longer-term conservation planning.

Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is essential, but so too is addressing the
existing threats faced by our birds of prey. Illegal shooting, poisoning, and collisions with buildings and vehicles continue to threaten these birds.

Reducing these human pressures could help build healthier, more resilient populations that are better equipped to cope with environmental change.

The white-tailed eagle is Britain’s largest bird of prey.
Diane Shaddick / Shutterstock

Continued monitoring is also essential – and this is where the general public can play an important role. Whether you are watching a red kite from your garden or spotting a kestrel while out on a countryside walk, you can record your wildlife sightings through citizen science platforms such as iNaturalist or BirdTrack. This can help scientists build a clearer picture of how bird distributions are changing.

These observations provide valuable data for future research, helping scientists
assess whether wildlife is responding to climate change in the ways that computer
models predict.

The recovery of many of the UK’s birds of prey is an important conservation success story. Ensuring that these recoveries continue in a changing climate will require us to think not only about where these birds live today, but also about where they might be able to live tomorrow.

Nothing to disclose.

articles.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be down to your blood sugar and genes
articles.summary:
Frozen shoulder can make everyday movements difficult – and it’s more common in people with diabetes. PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

Pain is often the first symptom, particularly at night. Over time, the shoulder grows stiffer. The flexible tissue that wraps around the joint, called the shoulder capsule, thickens and tightens, making it harder to move the arm.

That stiffness is a clue when a doctor or physiotherapist examines the shoulder. Even when someone else tries to move your arm for you, the movement is restricted. This is often most noticeable when they turn the arm outwards. The condition often improves, although recovery can take months or years.

Frozen shoulder is estimated to affect 2% to 5% of people and is most common between the ages of 40 and 60. It’s more common in women and people with diabetes are at higher risk. It can also develop after an injury or operation that stops you moving the arm as usual. Often there’s no clear trigger.

In type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. In type 2 diabetes, the body makes too little insulin or has trouble using it. In a 2014 study, nearly a third of participants reported a history of frozen shoulder. They had lived with type 1 diabetes for an average of 31 years. A 2021 study using genetic data also found evidence that type 1 diabetes increases the risk of frozen shoulder.

High blood sugar

A 2024 study using data from nearly 380,000 UK Biobank participants investigated whether raised blood sugar might help explain that link. Some inherited differences in DNA are linked to higher blood sugar. Because those differences are present from birth, they give researchers a kind of natural experiment. They can use them to estimate the effects of having higher blood sugar over many years, something a single blood test can’t capture. The study found evidence that persistently higher blood sugar makes frozen shoulder more likely.

One possible explanation is that sugar gradually changes the structure of the tissue around the joint. Sugars can react with collagen, a protein that gives the tissue much of its strength. The substances formed in that reaction can join collagen fibres together, making the tissue less flexible. In one small study of tissue taken during shoulder surgery, researchers found stronger signs of these compounds in samples from people with frozen shoulder than in samples from people with other shoulder problems. It’s a clue to how the tissue might stiffen. To find out whether these substances help cause frozen shoulder, researchers would need to know whether they build up before the shoulder stiffens.

Long-term high blood sugar has been linked to both frozen shoulder and Dupuytren’s disease, a hand condition that can make it difficult to straighten the fingers.
gdragan/Shutterstock

A 2021 study found five stretches of DNA linked to frozen shoulder. The strongest link was near a gene called WNT7B, which helps cells send signals to one another. Intriguingly, the same stretch of DNA has also been linked to Dupuytren’s disease, a condition in which tissue in the palm thickens and can pull the fingers inwards, making them hard to straighten. This suggests the two conditions may share some of the processes that cause tissue to thicken and tighten. The blood-sugar study found another link. Years of higher blood sugar appeared to make Dupuytren’s disease more likely, too.

For people with diabetes, persistent shoulder stiffness is worth bringing up at a routine appointment, especially if it’s starting to interfere with sleep or everyday tasks. For clinicians, it deserves attention alongside more familiar problems diabetes can cause in the eyes and kidneys. Whether improving blood sugar control can help prevent frozen shoulder or speed up recovery once it has developed is still an open question.
